We will have to defer our decision on that to some future occasion. The facts as far as I am aware are as I have stated. I do not propose to go into all the details of the case because they have been pretty well laid before the House by previous speakers. It suffices to say that the chief offender in all these disclosures would appear to be a former Minister of Customs, the Hon. Jacques Bureau. It would also appear that when the condition of affairs within the Customs department became revealed to the country, the government rewarded the Hon. Mr. Bureau for his services in debauching the department by appointing him to a senatorial position and placed in charge of the department a young and active minister in an effort to clean up that department.
I am not one of those who will readily condemn the present Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin). I have a good deal of sympathy for him. He inherited much of the present situation from the former chief of that department. The whole Customs department was debauched previously and perhaps it was too much to expect that the new Minister of Customs could set things right almost immediately. Therefore I say that I am prepared to be quite tolerant in my judgment of him. I shall be frank in saying that if there were no sins levelled at the government be-

5016	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Campbell
yond that of the charge against the present Minister of Customs, I would be prepared to say to the minister, "Go and sin no more," and to vote confidence in this government.
But the facts would prove that there is a good deal of responsibility on all, or nearly all, the colleagues of the minister besides the responsibility that is placed upon himself. I am not prepared to make him the sacrificial goat for all' the inherited sins of the party or the iniquities of that particular department. One of the things that I would hold against the minister-indeed I look upon it almost as his cardinal sin-is the fact that he would rise in his place in this House as a minister of the crown to defend the forme' Minister of Customs. If I was rather surprised at his action a few days ago, I was amazed when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) did the same thing yesterday. I think the least we might have expected was that these two hon. members should have dissociated themselves from the former Minister of Customs and been prepared to admit that a mistake was made in appointing him to the upper chamber.

On referring to the report of this committee, I find in the sworn testimony of Mr. Sparks he refers to a letter dated June 23, 1924, addressed to the Prime Minister and although it is rather long perhaps it is important enough for me to weary the House by reading it. It reads:
Dear Sir,-Confirming the writer's conversation with your secretary, Mr. McGregor, we would respectfully ask the opportunity for a delegation representing this association to lay before the government certain matters in connection with the wholesale smuggling of various classes of goods into Canada.
We think it would be desirable, should you grant this request, that the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Justice might be present, as the matters which we wish to lay before you affect these three departments.
We believe the Minister of Finance wrould be interested in the statement of our opinion that the loss of revenue will exceed $10,000,000 per annum.
As the prevention of smuggling comes under the Customs department, certain very important facts which we propose to put before the government in reference to the ineffectual methods now adopted by the Customs department will be of interest.
We shall also call attention to the fact that conditions in the ports, particularly in Montreal, are such that smugglers are practically immune from punishment.
The whole question of smuggling has become a national problem. It is seriously affecting business, and, as pointed out, causing a tremendous loss of revenue. This association for more than a year has studied this problem, and we would like to lay before your government a comprehensive statement covering the matter.

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Campbell
We would respectfully suggest that, if you are able to fix a date, it should be at least a week or ten days forward, as representatives from various parts of the country will require to be notified of the date set.
Trusting you will see your way clear to meet this delegation, and awaiting your early reply, we remain, Yours respectfully,
Canadian Association of Garment Manufacturers, per (Signed) R. P. Sparks,
President.
This is addressed to the Prime Minister under date of June 23, 1924. In the sworn evidence Mr. Sparks states that the deputation appeared before the government on the 6th August, 1924. When asked what ministers were present he answered as follows:
Right Hon. Mackenzie King, Hon. Jacques Bureau, Hon. Mr. Lapointe, Hon. Mr. Macdonald, Hon. Mr. Graham and Hon. Mr. King.
Yet, Sir, we find a number of these ministers denying absolutely on February 2 last that they had any knowledge of these conditions. To my mind that is amazing.
I am not going into many details but in my opinion the government had one opportunity to vindicate itself before the country, and I took occasion to point that out to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) privately. I even quoted an analogous instance in which the Scott government in Saskatchewan some years ago took action to clean up a corrupt state of affairs which was brought to their attention. A great deal of corruption had prevailed among members of their own party and among the civil servants, and the Saskatchewan government took steps to have the whole matter investigated. Did that government evade the issue? Did their members in the legislature stand up to a man and defend the malefactors? Not at all; the Premier said, "We want the fairest and fullest investigation, and we want everything that is wrong exposed."
By a royal commission.

It does not make much difference what means they took. They got all the facts and punished every man who was found guilty. Among those who were punished were three members of the party supporting the government and they served terms in jail for their crime. The result was that the Scott government was vindicated before the people of Saskatchewan, and when the next election came around they were returned by a larger majority than before. I as a supporter of that government felt proud to be of the same party. Now I say that this government lost an opportunity of vindicating itself by not going on record as being prepared to face the situation fearlessly 140-11-3181
and courageously. As I have told the Prime Minister, had he taken that course, I would have been prepared to vote confidence in his government and would have been glad to see them still in the treasury benches. If the government -had faced the situation as they ought to have done I would have felt that the ends of justice were being satisfied.
Now we are considering to-day an incomplete report; I say incomplete because it is a well known fact that the members of the Conservative party on the committee wanted to add an appendix to have certain recommendations embodied in the report, but the majority of the committee declined to accept that proposal. It is equally true that the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), representing the Progressive group on the committee, desired to have certain recommendations added to the report. His representations were also refused by the majority of the committee. For that reason I say that the report we have received in this House is incomplete.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre, in order to represent more properly the point of view of the whole committee, moved what I consider a very moderate amendment. If I were to find fault with the amendment I would say it erred on the side of moderation; and I think it expresses, if not in words at least in substance, just what the member for Peace River, the representative of the Progressive group on the committee, wanted to add as an appendix to the report. We in this section of the House have confidence in the hon. member for Peace River. We realize that having sat on the committee and heard all the evidence he is in a better position -than any other member in this group to understand the situation, and so far as I am concerned this amendment, meeting as it does in substance, as nearly as we could get it, the actual recommendations of the hon. member for Peace River, our representative on that committee, I feel I can do nothing but support the amendment.

Again we have brought 'before us the conduct of the former minister, Mr. Jacques Bureau, and let me say, as far as I am concerned, that the worst thing the .present government has done in connection with the whole matter was to put that gentleman in the Senate.
I quite agree with the hon. member in that regard. And by the way, I am glad to see that he is here now. I am sorry to have discussed him while he was absent, but I will repeat some of what I said for his benefit.

After all, we have to face the facts and there they are; there can be no question about that, and even in a larger sense I am not so sure that it is not so. Our party system is based on the principle of competition. We have two major parties competing for the spoils of office; we have a party in power fighting to retain office and a party out of power fighting to get into office. The group in this corner of the House was brought into being through a desire on the part of hundreds of thousands of the electors of Canada for something which would modify that situation, something which would make a definite change there. They believe a system could be worked out on the co-operative principle; they believe a system could be worked out whereby all the parties in the House could co-operate in forming a government and giving to this country the best brain and brawn of all parties. That, I say, was the ideal in the minds of hundreds of thousands of electors, the evidence of which we find in this corner of the House. Mr. Speaker, I cannot hope to entertain the House for long, but I trust I may be permitted to make a few observations. I do not intend to enter into the whole question, but having some knowledge of the Customs department, having been connected with it for twenty-one years in the city of Montreal, I think I speak with some authority.
The first observation I would make is that the action of the hon. member for Vancouver

Centre (Mr. Stevens) in moving for the appointment of this committee has been justified by results. There can be no question, and there is no doubt throughout this country, but that a public service has been rendered by the hon. member who was instrumental in securing the appointment of that committee. Sometimes we hear mention made of the cost of the investigation. I venture to say, without knowledge but with strong presumption, that the cost of the investigation has already been recovered to the treasury by additional revenue through the lessening of smuggling.
I would like to address the House for a moment on some of the recommendations of the committee. One of the recommendations urges a reduction in the number of ports. I tell hon. gentlemen of this House, and I speak with some experience, that that is impossible. All that the government can do is to refrain from opening more ports. They may have done the best they could, but still there are a few things which should commend themselves to the delicate conscience of some members of the Progressive party, who seem disposed to vote with the Tory party in order to avenge virtue and make all vice impossible. When it came out before that committee that the distilleries, those infamous dens of vice which the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Boutillier) painted in such dark colours yesterday, when it came out that these agencies of vice were helping the Tory party as well as the Liberal party, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) wanted to have the accounts opened in order to find the proportion of funds which went to the party of virginity and to the party of vice. But we are
5046	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bourassa
not in a position to know which cost the more, to get the favours of the Tory virgin or the caresses of the Liberal-well, I will not qualify it. The remainder of the committee, Liberals and Conservatives, the virtuous and the vicious, the avengers of moral right and justice as well as the depredators of public conscience, all joined together so that the people would not know how much more it cost to purchase the Conservative party than to purchase the Liberal party. Therefore, how can members of the Progressive party, whom I credit with a sincere desire to protect the morals of this country, justify a vote for this party more than the other? How can they justify themselves, any of them, in voting against the only possible suggestion so far made to keep the findings of this committee from the devil of political partisanship? This is just as bad for the morality of the country as the alcohol described by the hon. member for Vegreville, upon which a large number of the members of both sides do not show such horror when they are not making speeches; a number of hon. members even show in their speeches that they are not altogether convinced that whiskey is in itself vicious and illegal, even when it is drunk in contravention of the temperance laws of the virtuous province of Ontario.
One more point and I am finished. Another reason for which I think this inquiry should be pursued in every part of the country by a judicial tribunal instead of being passed upon by the House at this stage was pointed out by the Prime Minister. It brought shouts of protest from the other side when the Prime Minister said it was not sufficient to inquire into the province of Quebec. Let us have a real understanding; I have never stood for the protection of any crook in Quebec or elsewhere; I have perhaps denounced more malefactors of my own blood and race than any other public man in Canada, and I have taken them as they came, from both parties. But, on the other hand, using the same argument I made a few moments ago, if you want to have the public opinion of the people of Canada back of this attempt at reform, it must not be suspected that this inquiry was started or conducted-and I will not exaggerate anything-with as one of its objects, the idea of lowering the chances of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, or if that did not succeed, enabling Tory candidates elsewhere to denounce Quebec as a den of thieves, of smugglers and of immoral public men protecting vices and violations of law. I know that is not in the mind of the hon. member for West Hamilton; I know it 
is not in the mind of the right hon. leader of the opposition; but they know also that there are around them men prepared to do that sort of thing just as, if the situation were reversed, there would be camp followers of the Liberal party prepared to do the same thing.
The moment the inquiry was coming to the end of its investigation of Montreal affairs, one of the Tory papers of Montreal, I do not remember whether it was the Gazette or the Star, published a communication from Ottawa saying that the committee would soon end its inquiry because it had found sufficient evidence to demonstrate the system.

Might I ask a
question? Would the hon. gentleman for one moment be prepared to suggest that it was on the responsibility of any member of this committee that that paper should publish any such statement?

No, not at all; I have
just stated the contrary, and I have not corrected myself. I do not think it has ever entered the mind of any hon. member of the Conservative party whom I know; but circumstances are such that, if we adopt this report, the lower camp followers of both parties will be put by this House in a position to use that argument and counter-argument; and that should be avoided. Whether it means retaining this party in power or putting that party in power, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) knows that I always speak my mind, and I say that it is my earnest desire to prevent, if I can, a question of this nature being used to stir up racial prejudice and hatred.
I certainly have the same earnest desire.

I know my hon. friend has the same desire. There is no man in the province of Quebec, perhaps, who suffers more than the hon. member, at times, from the fact that he does not always find the same sympathy, from a purely social and individual point of view, amongst French Canadians as he would otherwise find if it were not for these base processes which have been resorted to time and again by both parties. If you create a political crisis of this issue without having completed your evidence, without having probed Toronto, Vancouver and any other town east or west in the same manner as has been done in the case of Montreal, without having brought before the bar of that committee all the miscreants, to whatever race or province they belong and whatever their political affiliations, you can-

Private Bills
not avoid it. I will not do it; the hon. member for West Hamilton will not do it in Ontario; the leader of the opposition will not do it as the head of his party, but it is bound to come. I have heard it said three hundred times at least since this committee first started: Yes, they are going to find out all about vice in Montreal, but they will not touch holy Toronto. I have heard that said in Montreal by honest people. There are a few things that have been said, and that are still being said, which justify some people in believing that there is some truth in that- not in the sense that the hon. member has rightly protested against, but truth in the sense that there are members of his party who are prepared to do that kind of thing. Already you see in various organs of opinion tentative suggestions to prepare the way for an anti-Quebec campaign, unless, of course, Quebec makes up its mind to help the Tory party, and then, of course, Quebec will be blessed just as it was blessed when it helped to throw down the Liberal party in 1911. I am not ashamed of having taken my share in that, but I admit that I felt ashamed afterwards of some of the men who made that fight with me. I have finished on that, but I repeat what I said the other day on war and peace issues, that it is far better now to face all the aspects of a position like this than to wait till the devils of racial discord are unleashed.
I sum up the whole thing. In the name of social justice and economic order, and for the sake of the proper administration of public affairs, the question whether this man or that has been indiscreet or not is a very small issue. The real issue is, since parliament has decided to get to the bottom of this, let us go to the bottom and let us come back next session, either under a Conservative or a Liberal administration; and in cool blood and after due reflection, let us pass such legislation and adopt such regulations as will command the confidence of the public conscience of the people of Canada at large, and not simply of one party or the other.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY

speechtext:
The House resumed, from June 22, consideration in committee of Bill No. 95, to incorporate the Red Lake and Northwestern Railway Company.-Mr. Heenan-Mr. Duff in the chair.

On section 1-Incorporation.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I wish to make one or two remarks arising out of some statements made by me when we last had this bill under consideration. I stated on a previous occasion that Manitoba was guaranteeing bonds to the extent of $25,000 a mile for a railway to go into this area. That statement seems to have been challenged by some hon. gentleman. Therefore I have tried to confirm this statement and I find it is correct. I have been unable, as I said.before, to obtain an actual copy of the bill; but looking up the files of the Manitoba Free Press in the Parliamentary Library I find that the day before the Manitoba legislature prorogued a bill to that effect was passed. This House would be creating a very bad precedent if it were at the present time to give its consent to the construction of another railway into the same area when one of the provinces of the Dominion has already agreed in some way, shape or form that I am unable to state to-night, to guarantee $25,000 per mile for the construction of a railway into that same area.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: What does the hon. member mean by a guarantee of $25,000 per mile?

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I believe a company was to be incorporated in Manitoba to build as far as the Manitoba boundary. If we look at a map of the Red Lake district we shall find that for the purpose of being able to get to a large centre of population for its supplies, the nearest point is the city of Winnipeg. On account of that fact I believe a company was to be incorporated to build a railway and Manitoba agreed to guarantee bonds to the extent of $25,000 per mile as far as the Manitoba boundary. That bill was passed during the last session of the Manitoba legislature which closed about the end of April.
This is something more than a mere branch line that we are asked to sanction the construction of to-night. I think we were told the last time the bill was under consideration that the charter was for a line to be built a distance of from 350 to 400 miles. A line 350 miles in length is more than a mere branch line. This bill has had very little consideration in committee. Another reason that was given for the construction of the line was the fact that there were 3,500 prospectors in the particular area that the railway was going to traverse. If this government is going to give charters for the construction of railways in every place in Canada where prospectors go in, we shall be doing nothing but issuing charters in all parts of the Dominion. I would prefer to wait in regard to this charter until

Red Lake Railway Company
another year, until we see what happens regarding the proposed connection with the Red Lake area from the city of Winnipeg.
Another reason why I think there is good ground for objection to this particular bill is that if we grant this charter, this railway will be given the right to traverse the same line and area as the Canadian National Railways traverse in northern Manitoba. It was stated here the other day that the Premier of Ontario had given his consent or voiced no opposition to this particular measure. I wonder why the promoters of this bill have not consulted Manitoba, which is vitally interested in the development of the northern part of Manitoba.
Manitoba is vitally interested in the completion of the Hudson Bay railway; yet this charter is to be given for a railway to go into The Pas and in the direction of the Hudson bay itself. In other words, although there are members in different parts of this House who doubt the feasibility of completing the railway to the Hudson bay because they think it will be a white elephant, yet there are others who come along at this juncture and want to build another railway into the same area. In other words in an area where some hon. members think it is impossible for one railway to pay, we are asked to grant another charter with the result that two lines may be built in the same area where it is contended that one line cannot pay. We should1 not be in too great a hurry to grant charters, because every time we grant a charter for a railway into a particular area we give the stamp of approval of parliament for the construction of that railway. I do not think it is a wise policy for this House to give the stamp of approval on railways until .we have far more information before us than we have at the present time.
I object to this charter being granted for the additional reason that Manitoba has not as yet had an opportunity of saying whether it is in favour of this railway or not, and until such time as I know what the opinion of the Manitoba government is I feel bound to voice my opposition to this measure. Those who are interested in the passage of this bill through this House would' be doing no hardship to the promoters of this company if they had to withdraw it at the present juncture and bring it before the House again at the next session of parliament. Very little would be lost because those who feel bound to voice opposition to this bill would perhaps be in some way convinced as to its feasibility. In the second place it would give Manitoba an opportunity of determining whether or not it should oppose the bill.
Another reason is the fact that it would enable us to see whether the company which is about to be incorporated in Manitoba will go ahead with its project, and whether Manitoba will be liable for the $25,000 per mile guarantee in accordance with the bill which was passed at the last session of the provincial legislature.
I feel I would have to voice my opposition this evening even to the extent of talking this bill out.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I have already spoken on this bill a couple of times, and I had it in mind to say just what the hon. member for ' North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) has said for me, but I hesitated to say it. I think anyone who has followed his remarks will now be of the same opinion that I am, namely, that this i3 a fight between the interests of Manitoba, which is desirous of building into Ontario, and the people of Ontario who desire to develop Ontario's own natural resources. That has always been the situation regarding the northern part of Ontario. Every time that we have endeavoured to develop northern Ontario we have obstruction from Manitoba, guardedly or unguardedly. The hon. member, contrary to some of his friends on the other side, has not argued in favor of public ownership in this regard, although he is a public ownership man, but he has argued that a private concern which has gone to the government of Manitoba and induced them to give a guarantee of $25,000 a mile for the building of a railway should receive consideration ahead of a concern in Ontario which desires to build a railroad into the Ontario mining area without any government guarantee. I think we have now a sufficiently strong case to show that no hon. gentleman opposite who has any regard for the province of Ontario and its development should vote against this measure. There is no question in my mind, any more than there is in the minds of the people of the part of Ontario affected that interests in Manitoba desire to tap the mineral wealth of Ontario and direct it into Manitoba channels.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: If that is the case will the hon. gentleman explain why the same interests are seeking to build a railway which will tap the natural resources of Ontario?

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: The "same interests" are not asking to tap the natural resources of Manitoba.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I beg to contradict the hon. gentleman. Authority is asked for in the hill to go to The Pas in the province of Manitoba.

Red Lake Railway Company
Mr. HEENAlN The object ie to build into the Red lake area first. In order to carry out that purpose they have to go through another province than Ontario. In view of that fact they have to get a charter from this government.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Why did they not go to the government of Ontario?

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: You had better put that question to the promoters of the bill. I cannot conceive that the rules of this House will permit the bon. member to talk out this bill, although he threatens he will do that. Surely the fate of the bill ought to be settled on its merits. If the rules of the House permit a bill to be talked out, without its being discussed on its merits, then those rules should be altered. When the measure was being considered in the Railway committee all kinds of obstacles were raised to its passage. First of all it was said that the opinion of the government of Ontario should be obtained with respect to it. This argument was urged by Ontario members and I have no complaint to make of that. Those hon. gentlemen wanted to know what the policy of the Ontario government was in connection with the bill. That information has been vouchsafed. Then a desire was expressed to know what the policy of the Dominion government and Sir Henry Thornton was in the same connection. That information has been given also. Finally the measure was remitted to the House, and now that we are in committee on it, instead of considering each clause of the bill on its merits there is discussion once more as to the principle embodied in the bill. Surely we ought to consider on its merits a bill which was passed by the Railway committee on a vote, I think, of nineteen to nine and been given a second reading by this House.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I cannot let some statements made by the hon. member pass without contradiction. He says that Manitoba interests are opposing this bill. Such statements are entirely out of place.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I wrote down the statement made by the hon. member and he said it was "obstruction coming from Manitoba interests." I am not obstructing the bill on behalf of any Manitoba interest; I am acting entirely in the interests of the province of Manitoba as a whole. It may be true that I am opposing some interests in the province of Ontario, but I really do not know at this hour

what interests are behind the bill. For all I know those interests may be interests of Backus and if that is the case I would oppose the bill a thousand times more strongly than I intend to do at the present time. So far as I know there is no obstruction from any interests of the province of Manitoba. Certainly I have received no instructions from anybody in that province to oppose the measure, but I do know this: a bill was passed at the last session of the Manitoba legislature giving a guarantee of S25,000 a mile towards constructing a railway to the provincial boundary; and unless there is some representation from the government of Manitoba agreeing to this bill I think I am perfectly justified in opposing it. What does the bill contemplate? It distinctly states that it is for the construction of a line to a point at or near Red Lake, a distance of about 100 miles, then in a generally northerly and westerly direction to a point on the Hudson bay division of the Canadian National Railway at or east of The Pas in the province of Manitoba. Now, if I am to take the correct inference from the statements of the hon. member, the only reason this clause was put into the bill was in order to obtain a Dominion charter. I think the statements of the hon. gentleman afford sufficient reason for the House to reject this bill. In other words, there is absolutely no intention on the part of this company of building into the province of Manitoba; there is no intention to build into the district of The Pas, and the granting of this charter would prevent the development of that district by others at some future time. Certainly no bill should be passed containing provisions which are not likely to be carried out. If the promoters have no intention of going to the province of Manitoba as the hon. member states, such a provision is merely camouflage.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: I did not say anything of the sort.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I did not say my hon. friend spoke of it as camouflage; that is my own statement. But he did say that the provision was put in for the purpose of getting a Dominion charter.
Now if the promoters are going to confine their operations purely to Ontario, why did they not go to the Ontario government and get a provincial charter? Then there would not have been any necessity for introducing the present bill in this House. The bill has been before the Railway committee on two occasions. The first time it was thrown out, I do not know for what reason. When it

Red Lake Railway Company
came back to the committee a second time it was passed and now comes before this House. We have as yet received no information as to who is behind the bill or who is going to finance the contemplated work; we have no information except what is contained in the clauses of the bill. I felt impelled to rise in order to contradict the statements of the hon. member, which statements, in my opinion, contain sufficient reason why this bill should be rejected.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I rise again to oppose this bill, not because of any personal or private interest but simply on general principles. I believe with the advocate of the measure that it should be accepted or rejected on its merits. I intend to speak briefly on those merits once more, but I would have thought that those who have this project in hand would have seen fit to withdraw the bill, seeing that it has been considered so many times by the Railway committee and by the House and has failed of acceptance. I am rather glad that this discussion has taken place because I believe it will result in the establishment of a railway policy for the Dominion which ought to be a guide for us in future applications for railway charters. The people of Canada have loaded themselves with a railway burden; they have plenty of trouble to ponder over for another generation or two owing to the indiscriminate granting of charters of this kind in the past throughout th' ~	The people of
this country are already sufficiently burdened with a debt of considerably over $2,000,000,000 through our railway system, and this has been brought about simply by small beginnings such as this charter represents.
Regarding railway service, this country is obligated to do two things. In the first place, we have been repeatedly told by financiers, stockholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and many others Who favour private ownership, that a 10 per cent dividend must be paid on the capital stock of that company to maintain the financial credit and integrity of Canada. If the present railway rates are not sufficient to do this, they must be raised, as they were in war time and since by the modification of certain statuory protection which the west enjoyed under the Crowsnest pass agreement. One thing is certain, we have been paying a handsome dividend to the privately owned Canadian Pacific Railway, while the government system has involved us in a deficit year after year, running all the way from $30,000,000 to $60,000,-
000.	We have been trying to make a great
transportation system out of these scattered branches of our Canadian National Railways. All these branches were indiscriminately chartered by past governments. The other obligation is to provide a service which, because of vested interests created by such indiscriminate railway construction, causes an overhead expense which cannot be met out of earnings, yet on the other system we are, through the people's industry, creating big dividends for private shareholders. This, I might say, is one of my chief objections to granting a charter for a railway which begins nowhere and ends nowhere, and is bound to be a burden to the country later on, when we shall have to take it over and perhaps purchase the charter from those who are now seeking it. The dividend on the privately owned system and the deficit on the government owned system is a super tax on the. earnings of the people. Both are the result of past mistakes, which this Red Lake project seems to repeat. I believe, Mr, Chairman, that had there been one complete system of government railways the railway year of 1925 would have shown a surplus instead of a deficit. That is, the people in primary production and through our export trade have paid for railway service over $60,000,000 more than was necessary had there been a complete system of government ownership of railways. This added to the saving which the elimination of duplication of service would have effected would have greatly lightened our burden of taxation to the extent, I believe, of about one-third of what is required for administration purposes this year, or about $120,000,000.
I have said that this parliament will have to formulate a railway policy. In confirmation of this let me quote a paragraph from a report of a royal commission on which Sir Henry Drayton and Mr. Acworth sat some few years ago. Regarding the ownership and control of our railway systems they advised:
That henceforth there shall ibe in Canada only two railway systems, the one consisting of the Canadian Pacific under its present management and control, and the other made up of the (present government railways, the Grand Trunk system, including the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Canadian Northern.
That the promoters of this wildcat scheme -for it is nothing more-for the exploitation of the people for private gain persistently push this project is evidence of the profits they expect to make when the charter is obtained. When this bill was before the , House the last time the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), I think, told us that the Premier of Ontario had no objections to it, and that the Canadian National Railway

Red Lake Railway Company
board was not even interested. But this is the people's business, and it is parliament that should decide whether or not this charter shall be granted, not the Minister of Railways or the board of the Canadian National Railways. I would ask hon. members to consider this bill very seriously and not grant a charter which will aggravate our railway problem, "or we are bound to be faced with heavier Jeficits if we indiscriminately grant charters >f this kind.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Clause 1, Mr. Chairman,
which is now under discussion, gives the names of the gentlemen seeking incorporation as John H. Cassidy, Charles OB. Hibbard, and Frederick R. Brown, all of the city of Montreal, and D'Arcy 'Scott, of the city of Ottawa, '"together with such other persons as may become shareholders of the company." I am wondering who is behind this scheme. I have become a little more suspicious since being informed a few moments ago that there is no intention of building this railway into the province of Manitoba, but merely from a point somewhere in the township of Wabigoon to a point touching Red lake somewhere in Ontario. If such is the case I think we should have a little more information than is contained in clause 1, and I would like to know if those promoting this bill can give us that further information.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext: Could I have the information I am asking for?

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
I cannot give any information other than what was given by the lawyer, Mr. D'Arcy Scott, when he was before the Private Bills committee; he gave the names of the bankers who were -behind it. My hon. friend said a while ago that if he thought Mr. Backus was behind it he would oppose the bill. I want to point out that Mr. Backus now has authority ito build a railway through the province of Ontario, and this proposed railway will be in competition therewith. I did not say, as the hon. member suggests, that it was not intended to build into Manitoba;
I-said it was necessary to go into two provinces before coming to this House -for a charter. The committee wan given full information as to the people behind the bill by the lawyer who had it in charge and by the promoter himself. I have nothing more to say; I am not going to talk my own bill out. If there are any questions, I will -be glad to answer them.

maintopic: RED LAKE AND NORTHWESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
Thei only information the hon. member can give is that Mr. Backus is not behind the bill, together with the additional statement that the committee was told of the bankers who were behind the bill, but that is not sufficient information. I think we should be given more than -the name of the lawyer who appeared before the committee and the names of three individuals of whom w'e know nothing. I see the lawyer's name mentioned here as one of the promoters of the bill; I believe it is quite usual in an application for a charter to have the name of the lawyer appear, but there is nothing to show that this charter if granted will not subsequently be disposed of to the highest bidder, and there is nothing in this bill to compel the company to actually construct one mile of a railway.
If it were only intended to construct this railway in Ontario that would be a very good reason for the bill being withdrawn and the required power obtained from the Ontario legislature. There would be very little time lost, because I -understand that the Ontario legislature meets early in- the year and continues in session for several months. Under this charter a period of twelve months is given in which construction must be commenced, and if that is not done the charter automatically lapses. But let me point out to the committee that the twelve months really amounts to two sessions of this House; after granting the -charter we will not know definitely whether or not anything has been done until after next session and the probabilities are that the charter would not be allowed to lapse but that this House would be requested to extend that tame. It is stated in one of the clauses that the sum of $100,000 must be spent by this company during the twelve months, but it does not mean that that amount must be spent in actual construction. That money can be easily spent in lawyers' and promoters' fees and in other matters of that kind; than the company can come back to the House and say they have spent the required amount of money and ask for an extension of the charter. That would establish a very bad precedent and I think we should demand something more than that.
In addition, no good reason has been presented as yet why a charter should be granted to cover the Manitoba area. A good case could be made out for a railway to enter the aRed lake area and possibly I would not oppose the bill, but when power is requested to go for a distance of 400 miles when 150 miles would be ample, I feel bound to offer my op-

Red Lake Railway Company
position, not merely because I am in favour of the principles of public ownership but because I feel that the promoters are asking for far greater power than they actually require. Unfortunately the promoters of this bill cannot give us the information we asked for, and I think that information is very germane to the whole bill. We have no assurance in any way that those behind the bill will proceed with the construction of the road, and I think under the circumstances we should not allow the bill to proceed at all until they first go to the Ontario legislature and have the measure passed there.
I wish, Mr Speaker, the letter from the Premier of Ontario to the committee in which he stated that he had no objection to this bill had been read to the House. I have not seen that letter nor have I heard it read here. It is rather strange that although the Ontario legislature began its session about the time this House met those responsible for this bill did not see their way clear to go to the Ontario house and secure the rights they are asking for here. It is one of the unfortunate things in our legislative structure that two bodies should have the power to grant charters for the construction of railways; that is another reason in addition to those enumerated by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) why we are in such difficulties at present. Here on the one hand we have all the provinces with authority to grant railway charters and give guarantees, and on the other hand we have the Dominion parliament granting exactly the same privileges. It has been stated that the only intention of the promoters is to tap the Red Lake mining area, and to give the prospectors there railway facilities. I think this is a purely provincial matter and should not have been brought before this House. From the statements submitted here it appears that the reason this charter has been asked for in this parliament is to overcome probably some legal technicalities, and if that is so I think it a very good reason why parliament should not grant a charter of this description. When the bill comes before the House we are informed by the hon. gentleman in charge of it that this is oiily put into the bill in order to overcome tertain technicalities, in order that the House itself might provide this company with a charter to construct the road, which is to be purely within the province of Ontario. If it is going to be entirely within the province of Ontario, the promoters of this railway had a perfect right to go before the Ontario legislature at its last session and secure a charter from that legislature, and then it would not
have been necessary for them to come to this House at all. W'e have had this bill before the House three times now, and several hours of valuable time have been taken up discussing it; it has been twice before the committee, and there does not seem to be much chance of it passing to-night.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mercier (St. Henri) for concurrence in the report of the special committee appointed to investigate the Department of Customs and Excise, the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. Mr. Stevens, and the proposed amendment to the amendment of Mr. Woodsworth.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in entering upon a
discussion of the .resolution, the amendment and the sub-amendment now before this House I feel a deeper sense of personal resiponsibiiity than 'I have felt on almost any other occasion in my life, which has been one of varied experiences and of grave responsibilities.
I represent, Sir, in this House a constituency in the province of Quebec, and it has been suggested that a vote againkt the subamendment and a vote for the amendment may be deemed to be a reflection upon the honour and reputation of that great province.
That, Sir, I specifically deny. I
9 p.m. have had intimate acquaintance with the leading men of that province during the past forty years. I
	,
have had the esteem of a number of my fellow-citizens in that province, and I have given to a greater number my esteem and personal affection, and therefore, although I am an English-speaking citizen of that province, and although I think there are a few in that province of its English-speaking cit-tizens who are better acquainted than 1 am with its language, its history, its literature and its traditions, I feel a sense of jealousy for its good name and reputation, and for that good name and reputation I am prepared. to stand at all times and on all occasions.
I also have, as I stated in an address which I delivered to this House on February 5th of the present session, a personal esteem not only for many of the members representing that province in this House, but for the members of the ministry who represent that province, and I think I can say, after a pretty careful reading of the evidence, that I do not find in that evidence any fact reflecting upon the personal honour of those members of whom I spoke on February 5th-the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries	(Mr. Cardin), the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon); nor do I suggest that the facts reflect severely upon the personal honour of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin), at the present time. In regard to the Minister of Customs, I felt all through this debate, having read the evidence, a measure of personal sympathy, in view of the facts which he had Stated to the House: that he had just entered upon his duties as a member of the government at the time that the Robichaud letter, so-called, had been received1 from the hon. member for Gloucester; that he had but a day or two in this city; that he -was pressed with the business of his new department; that numerous letters had been placed before him, and that it could not be expected that he could give that time and attention to the reading of letters that he might have done in less busy times and calmer moments. Although there were numerous discrepancies between the statement he made in that respect, as pointed out by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), and the evidence which he had- given personally before the Customs committee, and some discrepancies between his later statement and the statement he gave to the House when the motion for the appointment of that committee was made, yet after many years' experience in the courts, having been myself called1 upon to give evidence on many occasions, I am pre-

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Cahan
pared to ibelieve that the most intelligent witness in the witness box .may at times be unintentionally guilty of inconsistencies and verbal contradictions in his evidence. But what impressed me most, and what finally decided my opinion, was the statement of the hon. minister himself to this House in the debate on June 22. The member for Vancouver North (Mr. Donaghy), who sat on the committee and who is a political friend and associate of the hon. Minister of Customs, said in reference to the Robichaud letter:
The sting in the whole thing is contained in the letter which Mr. Robichaud wrote. We cannot hold anybody responsible for writing a letter like that other than the man who wrote it. Nobody with any sense of public honour would attempt to justify the expressions used by Mr. Robichaud in that letter and I am not going to attempt to justify them. My self-respect will not .permit it. The sting, I say, is in that letter and it is contained in these words in the letter which Robichaud wrote to Mr. Bureau, not to Mr. Boivin:
Mr. Aziz is of the highest help for us during this campaign, and we cannot do without his services.
That is the sting. I could well believe that if I had been in the position of the hon. Minister of Customs, with all the cares and distractions upon my mind which he had at the time, I might justify, on account of the conditions prevailing at the time, the instructions given through an officer of his department in the Aziz case. But the hon. Minister of Customs, in making his statement on June 22 to this House, said:
But I say now that if I had seen the request-
There had been discrepancies in his statement previously as to whether he had seen the letter and as to whether seeing the letter meant that he knew its contents:
But I say now that if I had seen the request and been cognizant of all the other circumstances my conduct would have been the same; I will say further that if this request had come to me from a Conservative member of parliament, my conduct and my reply would have been absolutely the same.
I do not say, I would regret to say, that the incidents of that case reflect severely upon the personal honour of the Minister of Customs, but the spirit which he showed in that vaunting statement to this House, sitting in judgment on this case, shows that at the present time, at least, he is not actuated by that spirit which should actuate a minister in his high position in the administration of the acts, matters and things that come from day to day before the Minister of Customs. I think the attitude he should have taken, in view of the facts that are before him now, and I think the attitude he should take now in view of that statement, is to withdraw from the ministry, to send in his resignation, to relieve,
so far as he can, the members of the government and the Prime Minister from the responsibility for approving the statement which he now makes-that even if he had been fully cognizant of the facts he would have acted in the same way as he did act under the circumstances. I have not lost my personal respect for the Minister of Customs. I know he is a younger man than myself, of great talents in many respects, talents which might be used to assist in the administration of the government of this country, talents which might be used in the public service, in other relationships and other spheres. But I do hope that a temporary absence from the ministry of this country will somewhat reform his spirit, will give him time for reflection, and that the time may come when he will withdraw those words and be in a position to resume again his high place in a position of public trust in this country.
The position in which the House finds itself to-night is this:	A committee appointed by
this House has heard the evidence and has made its report, a report which' has met with the express approval of the Prime Minister, a report which the Prime Minister says he and his government and his party are prepared to endorse by .their votes to-night. Paragraph 10 of the report so approved and so submitted contains this statement:
6. The evidence submitted to the committee leads to the general conclusion tihat for a long time the Department of Customs and Excise 'had been slowly degenerating in efficiency and that the process was greatly accelerated in the last few years. Aiptparentfly the Hon. Jacques Bureau, then Minister of Customs, failed to 'appreciate and properly discharge the responsibilities of his office and as a result there was a lack of efficient, continuous and vigorous control of subordinates by the headquarters staff at Ottawa.
Dealing with the administration of that department, the report also finds that in cases where a report was required from subordinate officers to comply and to conform with the well understood wishes of the minister, although in contravention of the facts then on the files of the department, subordinates were induced to make reports in order to sustain or to vindicate the action of the minister. That shows a thorough demoralization of that department at headquarters. On the other hand, with regard to the administration of that department in the matter of excise it is stated that orders in council had been passed, beginning on April 17, 1924, under which in the opinion of the committee unmatured spirits unfit for human consumption were freed for public consumption to the injury of the public health. Further this
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Cahan

is what the committee find in the administration of that department at the customs ports of the country:
10. The committee find that it is the common (practice of the department to grant clearances to vessels wholly or partly laden with liquor for the United States, or allegedly bound for a foreign port, ibut admittedly sailing to "nun rows", and that false landing certificates have been produced to obtain cancellation of bonds given for foreign export of cargoes so cleared..
In the evidence adduced before that committee and as showing that the reflections, suoh as they are, contained in the evidence and in the report, bear upon otlher provinces, bear with terrific force upon my native province of Nova Scotia, we have the evidence adduced that vessels laden with thousands of cases of liquor would leave the port of Halifax for ports in South America, in the United States or in the West Indies, in many cases voyages requiring weeks and months for their completion, and would return within twenty-four hours to the port of Halifax with landing certificates to release their bonds, landing certificates which never could have been obtained from Lima, Peru, from Nassau in the Bahamas or from any other port to which they sailed; and that officials and officers of the Customs department knew that in accepting those certificates they were giving facilities for forgery, fraud and perjury and admitting those fraudulent, false and perjured certificates as reliable documents on which and receiving which the Customs department could relieve the parties of the bonds which they had given to the department for the faithful export and landing of those liquors at the port at which they were alleged to be destined.
Those facts must have been known to every official of that department; they were current, in the press of the country. I know during the past summer when I was engaged before the courts in Halifax and in some proceedings there it was a gibe on the streets, a gibe of which you heard in the recesses of the courts of the city, that fraud, forgery and perjury were being committed with the knowledge of the customs officials of that great port. Although I regret to say it, and although I believe the general reputation of my native province is equal to that of Ontario or of Quebec, if there is any reflection upon a province in this report and in the facts adduced before the committee and found to be true in the report, it reflects as greatly upon my native .province of Nova Scotia, where public morality as a whole is as high as in any other province of Canada.

Why did the facts which were alleged come from the city of Montreal? Montreal is not the province of Quebec. Montreal is a great commercial city, it is true; but the high public morality, the virtue of private living and life which characterize that great province, may not. be so well exemplified in some of the worst quarters of the great city Of Montreal. But because we have wrong-doing in some of the purlieus of Montreal I defy any intelligent man to say that the bringing of those facts to light from the purlieus of that city casts a reflection upon me or my fellow citizens of Montreal.
In addition, the report of 'the committee which has been approved by the Prime Minister and by the government, as I said, asks for further investigation into the facts, and I as a citizen of Quebec wish to know what are the facts with regard to Windsor, Vancouver and other ports of entry in the western provinces. The committee, headed by one of the most intelligent young men representing my city in this House, reported as follows:
12. . . . With reference to the distilleries, the committee has not had time to investigate them all. The committee recommends that a thorough audit and examination be made of the records and accounts of all the distilleries.
14. The committee recommends that the conduct of the officers at the port of Windsor, Ontario, and other important ports, should be further investigated and that the services of such of them as are found guilty of evasion of duty should 'be dispensed with.
The committee knew well that having been engaged for some five months in this inquiry they 'had not completed all the evidence available, and they urgently demanded, so far as they could, that this House and the government should insist upon further inquiry and investigation being made. But the government has the full duty and1 responsibility with regard1 to that investigation. The government has the authority, without any further legislation or direction from this House, to appoint a royal or other commission under the Inquiries Act to make full, careful and complete inquiry into all these transactions at other ports.
Now in regard to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) the House is asked to approve of the following:
The evidence further discloses that ministerial action has been influenced by the improper pressure of political associates and friends of the minister, or acting minister, administering the department, resulting in the suspension and in some instances the abandonment of prosecutions against those charged with violation of the statutes, and in the loss of revenue to the country. Moreover, successful appeals have been' made to

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Cahan
the minister and acting minister administering the department to improperly interfere with the course of justice 'between the conviction of the offenders and the execution of judgment thereon.
With regard to that I wish to say that the argument that under previous administrations there has been wrongdoing, where corrupt acts have been committed by members of the ministry or employees of the department, is not convincing to me. Under the conditions which prevail in Canada to-day-and I will leave the province of Quebec-under the conditions which prevail in my native province of Nova Scotia the rum traffic, unhindered, is ruining homes and ruining lives, and steps should be taken to enforce the law in that province. As to the appeals which have been made under previous administrations, all I have to say is, that although the evidence adduced by the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) is not convincing to me until I have read and analysed it, previous wrongdoing does not justify the action of this House in refusing to condemn similar practices today. If we are coming to the stage that the public honour of this country is not to be maintained, that the moral spirit of this country is not to be maintained, because in times past there has been wrongdoing by Conservative administrations which justifies wrongdoing by a Liberal administration today, then I say I am prepared to abandon every other political relation I 'have in life and join' some independent party in this country who will see that the law is properly administered, irrespective of what 'has been done in the past either by Conservatives or Liberals.
The amendment further declares that:
The Prime Minister and the government had knowledge for some considerable time of the rapid degeneration of the Department of Customs and Excise, and their failure to take prompt and effective remedial action is wholly indefensible.
I think it has been shown by the letters produced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself that his government were very fully informed, as I will show in a few minutes, of the material facts of the case. Then the amendment declares:
The conduct of the present minister of the department, the Hon. George H. Boivio	is utterly unjustifiable.
His action was unjustifiable if he had been thoroughly informed of the facts; and now that he, before the high court of parliament, has declared that his action would have been the same if he had known the facts in all their ramifications and all their bearing, I have no hesitation in saying his conduct was not justified. And yet when I say that I make this reservation; I do not believe that
is a finding, as hon. gentlemen opposite have said, to the utter dishonour of the Minister of Customs. I hope and believe that when he has had time to reflect upon his admissions before this House he will regret such admissions and regret the spirit which prompted them as much as I, standing in my place in this House to-night, sincerely regret them.
Next the amendment declares:
Your committee deplores the practice, as revealed by the evidence, of certain men influential in public life to direct appeals to the minister to relax and depart from the proper administration of his department for reasons of political expediency.
Your committee is of the opinion that this practice is detrimental to the best interests of the country and prejudicial to the administration of the department.
Now, the sub-amendment, which Your Honour has declared to be in order, in the main asks that clause 6 in the amendment be deleted and in lieu thereof the following inserted as an addition:
Your ccxmmi'ttee deplores the common ipractice, as revealed by the evidence, of members of parliament and others appealing to the minister to relax the regulations of the department for personal advantage or (political exped iency.
I entirely agree with that statement, but why, by inserting that, should we remove all reflection upon ministers of the crown who give effect to such appeals, and without whose definite action such appeals would be entirely in vain? Why is it that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth), who proposed that subamendment,, wishes to remove that reflection upon the government of the country, and every reflection upon a minister of the crown who had given effect to sordid, personal appeals of that character? Therefore my position is this: that with respect to the contents of the subamendment proposed1 I would be prepared to vote m favour of those in the main, but they can and should only be given effect to as an addition to and not as a substitution for the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). And if the government wish to give full effect to the opinion of this House I believe they will now agree and Will solicit the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to withdraw the subamendment os a substitution for the amendment and add it to the amendment in order to give it full and complete effect. In so far as the subamendment proposes that a royal commission should be appointed in order to continue the investigations, that is a matter entirely within the discretion of the government; it has full power and authority to appoint such a commission.
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Cahan

But, Mr. Speaker, although the Prime Minister has declared his approval and the approval, I understand, of his government, of the general recommendations and the statements contained in the report of the committee that:
The evidence submitted to the committee leads to the general conclusion tihat for a long time the Department of Customs and Excise had been slowly degenerating in efficiency and that the process was greatly accelerated an the last few yeaxs.
Nevertheless he suggested, and in fact quite frankly stated, that it is not within the competence of this House, as a political and partisan body, to judge of that report and to render a verdict upon it. No man in this House or in this country is more fully informed than the Prime Minister of the great agitations which were carried on from decade to decade in order to achieve responsible selfgovernment in the provinces of Canada; no man is foetteT informed than he of the principles which underlie responsible self-government in this country. And we are sitting in judgment to-day because there is no other court in this country, and no other court can be constituted without an almost complete abrogation of the constitution, which can be empowered to take the place of this House in judging of that report and finding a verdict upon it. In September last the Prime Minister appealed to whom? To the general electorate of this country for their support by returning to this House of Commons, if it was possible to be obtained, a majority supporting him and the party which he has led for so many years, and with which he has been identified for almost the whole of his later life-the party of which, I might say he has been a distinguished member, and in which he has rendered to this country many eminent services. The parliament assembled here today is the result of the recent verdict of the people, and the government, the members who form the administration, are responsible to this parliament and must justify their acts before it. Parliament is vested with the right of legislation, of enactment by statute, for the government of the country. Parliament enacts the law under which the administration is carried on, but the Prime Minister and his colleagues are responsible to this House, and to this House alone, when it is in session, for the efficient and faithful administration of those laws. In the earlier weeks of the session I sat in this House and heard such discussions as would lead1 members to believe that the making of our laws is of paramount importance, of more importance than their administration ; but I submit that the administration of the laws after parliament has enacted them

is a duty and responsibility of this government, and that those laws will be utterly ineffective and inoperative unless that administration is duly and faithfully performed.
Now, this theory and practice of the constitution is endorsed, in part, by the right hon. Prime Minister in his recent address. He says:
According to our theory of government, the Minister of Customs is responsible for the administration of the affairs of that department.
But the Prime Minister failed to state that he himself and his colleagues in the ministry are responsible to this House and to this country for the efficient administration of each and every department of government. That responsibility and that duty cannot be denied by the Prime Minister and those associated with him. Now, did the Prime Minister have knowledge of the conditions existing in this country, conditions which were known generally throughout the length and breadth of Canada? Not knowledge, I suggest, of every specific detail, but did he have knowledge of existing conditions sufficient to put him and his colleagues upon inquiry and upon investigation? If he had such general knowledge and notice, I say he is responsible to this House for not ordering such an effective inquiry as would have brought the details more directly to his notice. The Prime Minister admits that after the negotiation of the agreement between this government and the government of the United States in 1923-
-the attention of the government was drawn for the first time to the growth of the smuggling evil as it affected commercial interests in this country.
That was in 1923, nearly three years ago. Yet I say to-night-and I do not think my statement can be denied-the Prime Minister cannot point to one single fact in evidence in this case which discloses that the government took effective measures to render administration of the customs more effective. A delegation representing a number of the large manufacturing and commercial interests of the country informed the Prime Minister and his colleagues of the existence of these great evils in the Customs administration.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: What date was that?

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
After 1923, the minister says. What attitude did the government take? Let me read the Prime Minister's own statement of the government's attitude. Referring to this delegation that came to meet the members of the government, he says:
Did the government say: No, we have our own preventive service, our own Customs department, our own officers. We ourselves will look after the suppression of smuggling and the -protection of the revenue laws.

Customs Inquiry

Mr. Cahan
I submit that is what this government are elected to do, that is what they must do to carry out their oath of office, in order faithfully to perform the responsibilities and duties which rest upon them. That is what they must do if they are to maintain a good account with the parliament and with the House of Commons of this country. And what does the Prime Minister say? The Prime Minister says the government did not take that position, and I say that in not taking that position the government were recreant in their solemn trust and duty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend is drawing an entirely wrong inference from those words.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I do not want to do an injustice to my hon. friend, but I am going to elaborate my argument and I think he will see that I am not straining his words unduly. If I do so I regret it very much, but I am going on. The government entirely abnegated their responsibilities and duties; the government under the direction of the Prime Minister took the indefensible position of placing upon those very men who formed the delegation the duty and responsibility of what? First of making suggestions which would most effectively deal with the situation. The delegation asked among other things for more effective legislation and the government, feeling no particularly urgent responsibility, asked the delegation to draw up the measures which in their judgment it was essential to have enacted. And then further he says:
The government met that request by asking the Commercial Protective Association to draft such legislation as its officers thought would be most effective.
Then the Prime Minister says to this House:
Now I ask, could the government -possibly have taken a more effective way of dealing with the -problem than by requesting those most concerned to draw up the legislation themselves?

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Let George do it.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Yes, let George do it. What were the existing conditions at that time? The Prime Minister has quite fully and frankly informed us; he says:
The country was face to face with a condition in relation to smuggling of such a magniture as few could comprehend.
But the Prime Minister leaves us to understand that he fully comprehended it. He had all the agencies of government at his command and yet failed by one single administrative act, one single effort, to administer the existing laws pending further legislation which would tend to mitigate these evils;
he left it to a private association of business men to draw up and submit the additional legislation. More than that, he left it to this private association to supplant the Department of Customs in the administration of the law at the outports. Was not this a complete or almost complete abnegation by the Prime Minister and the government of the duties and responsibilities of the high offices which they respectively hold?

Does my hon. friend wish the House to infer that in his view the government should have declined to co-operate with the protective association?
M-r. CAHAN: No, certainly not. I am going to deal with that in a moment. But when before in the history of this country did a government abnegate their duties and responsibilities; when did they ever fulfil the high trusts of their office by placing the administration of a department of government in the hands of a private association of business men? Again in the letter of February 4, 1925, which the Prime Minister read, Mr. Sparks informed the government that:
iSmuggiling and undervaluation for duty purposes were causing an immense loss of revenue and seriously interfering with the business of legitimate traders and manufacturers.
Yet no active administrative efforts were made to protect the treasury by checking these evils. And the Prime Minister adds:
Assuredly the protective association brought to the attention of the government the evils of smuggling as they have described .them.
But it was not only additional legislation which was urged by this delegation who approached the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister quotes a letter from Mr. Sparks dated February 26, 1924, as follows:
Might I take the opportunity of stating that after four months of investigation by a staff of trained criminal investigators-
Referring to investigators employed by the merchants and manufacturers association.
-we are convinced that at least half of the smuggling now going on oouild ibe prevented within a month by an energetic policy on behalf of the department.
But in the record of evidence taken by tlhaifc committee I submit there was not one single effective administrative measure taken by the government in the course of these three years to mitigate these evils and to protect the commerce of this country. Again on April 8, 1925, Mr. Sparks wrote to the Prime Minister as follows:
Smuggling on this continent has become a huge industry. . . . After months of investigation by trained investigators we have no hesitation in saying that this traffic constitutes a national problem of the very first importance.
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Cahan

Then the Prime Minister himself says:
I regarded tlhis as probably the greatest prohlem which the country has before it at the present time.
Again let me state that on July 13, 1925, almost a year ago, the president of the Toronto Board of Trade wrote the Prime Minister urging upon him and his government that in the reorganization of the preventive service the dominant note, to quote his words, should be the strict enforcement of the law in the interests of the lawful commerce of the Dominion and an increased national revenue which, in turn would be reflected in an improvement in economic conditions generally. Yet still not a single direct effort was made by the Prime Minister and his colleagues to secure a more effective administration of the law, although at that time they had secured from this House an amendment to the law with more stringent provisions, and a vote of this House supplying all the necessary funds to carry that law into effect. The returns brought down recently in the public accounts show that they so neglected their duty that they did not even make use of the appropriation which this parliament had placed at their disposal for the efficient administration of the law passed in 1925, "But," the Prime Minister says, "We gave the association government detectives; we paid for those detectives and told them to use those detectives and let them report to you"-to Mr. Sparks. Yet in this House, if I understood the Prime Minister correctly-and I am prepared to withdraw the statement if he denies it-he spoke of disloyalty to him and to his government on the part of one of the officials loaned to Mr. Sparks, and who was instructed to report to Mr. Sparks.
