speechtext:
Were they? And so the
Prime Minister and his colleagues disregarded their responsiblities as members of the government of Canada, and proved, I repeat, recreant to the trust which was imposed on them, and left the administration of the custom laws of this country in the hands and under the control and direction of a private mercantile association. Then to this body of private gentlemen who, at the government's request, were in fact usurping the functions of the government of the country, the Prime Minister describes his attitude as follows:
What attitude did I take towards him?

He is referring to Mr. Duncan, who was then in the employ and under the direction of this private association of merchants:
What attitude did I take towards him? What attitude did the Minister of Finance take? We said to him: Thfis business which you are on is a serious one foir the country. We give you full latitude to do anything and everything you want to do or think ought to be done.
What was that but the re-establishment ir>
this country of an irresponsible body to whom some of the chief functions of administration in this country had been assigned and entrusted by the Prime Minister of the country? And so I say that the government of this country by a responsible cabinet, under 3 responsible prime minister, ceased to function in Canada, and the system of responsible government, the system of parliamentary institutions, which are the only hope and stay of Canada, were degraded, step by step, until they have reached the contemptible position in which some members of this House would by their speeches place them to-day.
What are we told to-day? We are told that although this ministry is responsible to this House and to this House alone, although there is no other body in this country, judicial or otherwise, to which they can submit themselves and still maintain responsible government in this country-we are told by them, now that parliament has so degenerated, that we are unfit and incapable of judging of the merits of a report submitted after six months of investigation by members of a committee on which the government controlled the majority. We are told that we are unfit to consider and decide upon that report. When, I would like to know, was there ever a precedent in the history of any province of Canada since responsible self-government was granted, when was there ever a precedent in the history of the proceedings of this parliament, when the only prospect held out to the country was, on the one hand, government by a private committee of mercantile men, or on the other, authority being vested in some judicial committee or commission appointed by the government themselves to judge of their own conduct, because parliament is unfit to so judge, as parliament has done ever since we have had responsible government?
The Prime Minister appealed to this country, and a minority of this House were returned pledged to support him. He has appealed to this House now, and this House alone can decide. There is no other tribunal judicial or otherwise, that has or possibly

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Kennedy (Peace River)
could have jurisdiction to decide in this matter. Upon this House, and upon this House alone, rests the responsibility, and the sole responsibility, and no matter what may be our individual capacities we are derelict in our duty, we forswear our oaths of office and our pledges to the country, we are recreant to that duty which is placed upon us by our institutions, if we decline to-night so to decide.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up the time of the House at any great length. I merely wish to state what my position will be when the time comes to vote on the amendment to the amendment, and on the amendment.
I have listened with a great deal of care to most of the debate. My position has changed somewhat since I moved the amendment in the committee. The majority of the committee was unable to agree to it. The Conservative members of that committee moved a certain amendment, and I also
10 p.m. moved an amendment representing my views at that time. After listening to the debate I not only think that my position in the committee was justified, but I feel that when the opportunity presents itself I must vote for the amendment that has been moved in this House.
In section 6 of the report, which has been referred to quite often in the debate, I find the following-and to this, of course, every member of the committee agreed:
The evidence submitted to the committee leads to the general conclusion that for a long time the Department of Customs and Excise had been slowly degenerating in efficiency and that the process was greatly accelerated in the last few years. Apparently the Hon. Jacques Bureau, then Minister of Customs, failed to appreciate and properly discharge the responsibilities of his office and as a result there was a lack of efficient, continuous and vigorous control of subordinates by the headquarters staff at Ottawa.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, I moved that Mr. Farrow, the Deputy Minister of Customs and Excise, should be discharged. The majority of the committee recommended that h'e should be retired. My reason for objecting to that was simply this: We had recommended that a number of the officials in the Department of Customs should be discharged, and I could not see any difference between the position of some of these officials whose names are mentioned in the report and that of the deputy minister under whom the department had so rapidly degenerated during the last few years. I am very much opposed to the distinction that is drawn between
individuals who practically are all guilty of the same kind of conduct and the same inefficiency in performing their duties, simply because one happens to draw $2,000 a year and the other $10,000.
That very position leads me still further. I find that while the position of a minister in the government is somewhat different, I have to vote for as near the same kind of censure of him as I am constrained to vote for with regard to Mr. Farrow. Certainly if the deputy minister was guilty he should be held responsible, in a large measure at least, for the degeneration in efficiency of the department. This is much more true of the ex-Minister of Customs, Hon. Jacques Bureau. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the government itself has to accept responsibility for the degeneration in efficiency of that department. This, of course, I regard as a very serious matter for the government, and it is the chief reason why I feel that I must vote for the amendment after the subamendment is disposed of. The Department of Customs is practically as important a branch of government as the Canadian National Railways, if you like to call them a branch of the government. The total revenues of the Canadian National Railways amount to a little over two hundred million dollars annually. Under the Customs department, taking the various branches together, we obtained a revenue in 1924 of nearly three hundred million dollars. Does anybody believe that we would be justified in voting confidence in the government if it could be said that under the management placed and left at the head of the railways there had been or was a rapid degeneration in efficiency during the last few years? That is the thing that appeals to me as being so serious in connection with this matter. The whole evidence bears on this question and justifies that conclusion.
We have been told that the government is bad, that it has made some very bad mistakes, and that it is true of previous governments that we have had. That may be. We have not the privilege of dealing with the previous government to-day, but we have the responsibility of dealing with the present government. We have been told what will happen if the hon. members who form the official opposition come into office. Well, I wonder if we are going to be able to keep them out of office. They very nearly succeeded in defeating the government during the last week or two, and I do not want, Mr. Speaker, to establish a precedent here that any government can expect the confidence of this House even if it has allowed the chief revenue collecting department of the government to degenerate rapidly
5062	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Macdonald (Antigonish)
in efficiency. It seems to me-and that is the reason I differ with most of my colleagues here-that the government that allows that to happen must face something more than a severe tongue-lashing in the House of Commons, and the only weapon we still have, and the only weapon that governments fear, is a vote of want of confidence.
I would trust that if the amendment to the amendment does not carry, it can be moved as an addition to the amendment. As it stands at the present time I find that it will be necessary to vote against the amendment to the amendment and support the amendment, not *that I disagree with the amendment to the amendment so far as its form is concerned, but because of its position and relation to the amendment. Not that I altogether agree with the terms of the amendment, but I do agree with it in so far as it is a vote against the government, and having regard to the evidence and to what has happened in the department during the last few years, I can conscientiously cast my vote only in that way.

Before the motion is
put I rise to speak more of a matter of privilege than otherwise. My hon. friend from Kent, N.B, (Mr. Doucet), in his address the other night, referred to me as being one of those who participated in the stopping of prosecutions for smuggling. I want to mention a circumstance that occurred in June 1925. A portion of the permanent force were in Glace Bay, Cape Breton. They had an officer's mess there. These officers had some liquor. This liquor was seized, I do not know by what authority, Whether federal or provincial. Everybody who knows anything about the life of officers, on active service or otherwise, knows that the mea is an institution which has been maintained by them from time immemorial. When the liquor was seized one of the officers happened to be going to Montreal, and came on to Ottawa. He reported the matter to the department and stated-and the officers of the department sustained the point-that under the king's regulations the mess supplies were immune from seizure by civil authority. I simply transmitted to the department the position

these gentlemen took in regard to this officers' mess. I never inquired what the decision of the department was, and I never knew what it was. Further than that, I had nothing whatever to do at any time with regard to this question of the smuggling of liquor or smuggling of any kind. I merely wish to say that if the innuendo which was contained in my [DOT]hon. friend's reference to me was of the same character as was made to some of my colleagues, then there have been a great many innuendoes in this discussion that are without foundation.
Mr. MALCOLM MicLEAN (Melfort):	I
do not intend to take up much time of this honourable House, but I wish to make some remarks before the vote is taken. If I might be permitted to digress a little bit, I would like to tell hon. members a story. I am reminded of two boys who were working in a law office. They met one day and one said to the other, "Johnny what do they pay you at the office?" Johnny said, "Four dollars a week, what do they pay you"? The other boy said, "$1,000 a week". Johnny says, "Aw go on, you're talking." The boy said to him, "No, I am not, they pay me $3 a week in money and $997 in advice." I feel something like that boy. As a new member of this House I am bewildered by the flow of legal lore and the advice that has been given particularly during the past few days, but generally through the session,. The legal advice and information that have been given us are enough to bewilder an ordinary, plain person trying to solve problems coming before this House on the basis of experience and common sense and by assiduously studying them. So to-night, as I look over the debate of the past few days and the issue at stake herein, I find that I must endeavour to differentiate between the material that has been displayed and the legal verbiage that has been thrown around it.
Time after time in this House I have heard clever lawyers such as the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) argue the case as if they were prosecutors in a court-house prosecuting some law breaker. I appreciate much the excellence of the wisdom and learning given to us by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George and the plane on which he spoke. But habits of the court room are hard to break, and apparently the intention on his part and on that of many hon. members opposite was not to make the matter plain and clear to us, but to ensure that a verdict would be given against the defendant.

Custom* inquiry-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
When first these charges were made in this House some months ago, I was surprised that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) should in his laudable desire to suppress smuggling in this country, go all the way to Montreal, Rock Island, to Beebe and these other places of which many of us had never heard before and tell us about the lamentable conditions existing in the customs administration there. I would have thought that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, coming from the city of Vancouver, a city which through the press and other methods of spreading information has been notorious for smuggling, booze running and dope peddling for many years back, would have first started to clean up near his home where we are told that charity begins. I would have thought, I say, that there where it was easier for him to get information he would have endeavoured to start the cleaning up process.
I found, however, that there was something else to it than that. I found that in addition to the smuggling of liquor out of Canada and other commercial goods into Canada, there was the smuggling of something worse, something that in my opinion the Canadian people will feel less like forgiving even than the smuggling of liquor out or the smuggling of other commercial goods in. I refer to the smuggling of secret information, secret reports, confidential reports, prepared by trusted employees of this government for the benefit of the public and the administration generally in enforcing the observation of the law and in bringing evildoers to justice. These reports, according to all the information that has been given us in connection with this matter during the past few days, were smuggled from their rightful place in the possession of the government into the hands of the chief political attacker of the government at this time. While I am not excusing the smuggling of liquor or other goods into the country and other goods out of the country, these are material things, the value of which can be reckoned accurately in dollars and cents. But when parts of the civil service of Canada, the secret agents of the government who are paid to get information on which the laws can be upheld, are debauched to the stage where they are willing to allow their information to be smuggled to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre or any other hon. member, that is a sad state of affairs and the people of this country are not going to think lightly of it.
Information given out during the course of this debate has shown that all the disclosures in the Customs Inquiry committee on smug-14011-321
gling in two months and a half, prepared for and paid for by the government and handed to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, was that based on the famous Duncan report. Is there anything so infamous in the history of the department as that this information which was prepared an'd paid for by the government should be handed over for political purposes and that the service should be debauched in this way? Yet, hon. gentlemen qpposite smirk and smirk as they sit in their places and think lightly of it, while they talk of some youngster who brought in some celery, bread and other things.
I notice another hon. gentleman of the legal profession making notes, and I know he will get after me in good style; but I am satisfied that to-night I have in mind the outlook of the people of Canada rather than the heated and biased outlook that it is almost impossible to keep away from after 'six months of political warfare in Ottawa, where intrigue runs strong, where lobbying has been developed to the fine art at which it stands, where efforts have been made such as we had an inkling of in the debate-yes, desperate efforts made to swing members this way or that but generally I think to swing them away from the thing their constituents in many cases want.
This attack on the government through the Customs investigation and now through this report is not a new thing at all. All during this session and the session of last year hon. gentlemen opposite have been making these attacks on the government. The government have been accused of almost everything under the sun. If they were not accused of anything that was bad, it was because their opponents apparently overlooked it. At the start of the session they were accused of paralyzing industry, bringing the country tu the brink of ruin.

The hon. member says that is right. Yet he has helped to hold the House here for six months and has not suggested anything to assist in remedying that state of affairs. All through this session attacks have been made on the government. First hon. gentlemen opposite tried economic attacks. This House was well fitted to deal with that, because of the fact that the House had gathered in members from 245 seats throughout the country who knew the exact conditions in their constituencies and were thus able to compare them with those of last

5064	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
year, the year before and six months ago. So the economic attacks on the government failed.
They brought political attacks on the government and again for the same reason members who had gathered from all parts of the Dominion were able to judge of their value and they failed. They accused them of being a government held in office by bribery, barter and many other terms that might not be parliamentary so that I will not repeat them. These political attacks were made on the government time after time and they failed. So they decided on another form of attack and, true to Tory traditions, they decided to bring it on moral and uplift grounds. This - is not a ne\v thing at all, but it is something that would almost make the angels w'eep to hear of a Tory opposition in the city of Ottawa in the year 1926 attacking the government of the day on high moral grounds. This is a form of attack that they have made on different Liberal governments at various times throughout the Dominion and people have reached the stage where they very easily discount such methods. But when they brought this new moral attack on the government they coupled with it an extremely strong barrage of legal argument, and in this I will admit the remainder of the House is at a disadvantage over members of the opposition. They have now spent days and weeks at different times during this session giving us legal arguments. If we could turn these arguments into good cash value we certainly would be enriched. But we cannot do that, because there is no value in them. If you weigh them dispassionately you will agree that there is no market for these legal opinions that we have been getting. This is an old method, Mr. Speaker, to break down co-operation between the various groups that have combined to carry on the government of the country. When they cannot be broken down directly on the economic or political isues involved, it is a first class plan to use moral and "uplift" arguments. If we cast our eyes back a few' years to the Motherland where co-operation has been employed between different political parties, we find the same plan tried; we find that an issue such as we are debating to-night has been interjected in order to try and cause disruption. I remember the government of Mr. Asquith, I think it was, being defeated in 1895. A number of groups were working together, and the government was defeated after a very heated debate, on the cordite question. The Tory politicians made the welkin ring 
with their predictions of the danger to which the empire was exposed because there were not sufficient supplies of cordite on hand. Well, the government w'ere defeated, they went out of office, and their opponents took their place, and within a few weeks it was shown that no addition had been made to the cordite supplies of the country although it was proclaimed by the Tories that there was a calamitous shortage. However, the Tories achieved their purpose. They got into power and the country got ten years of Tory misrule, including the Boer war, as a result of that famous debate on the cordite question.
Throughout this session hon. gentlemen opposite have been taunting the government with being in a minority and of having to make promises that were not in the interests of the country in order to secure support. Moreover the Progressives have been condemned likewise in the worst possible manner for co-operating with the government. Yet to-night we find hon. gentlemen opposite applauding some of the former allies of the government who have announced that they are going to support this amendment. I say this is all part of the game. From the political point of view it may be a very fine-game but it will not be endorsed by the people of this country who have to pay the bills and who have sent members down here in order that they should co-operate in the carrying on of the administration of public affairs; it is a mighty poor game from the standpoint of the interests of the country.

Yes, quite sure. But let me say this: the courteous thing for any hon. member when asking a question is to rise and not remain in his seat.
We have had some memorable speeches on the legal aspect of this question. I am not going to enumerate them, but I have something to say to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. That hon. gentleman is not a lawyer but he gave a long address and no doubt,
JUNE 25, 1926	506-c.
Customs Inquiry-Mr. McLean (Melfort)
from his own point of view a very effective one. I noticed, though, that he did not touch on the smuggling conditions in his own city which, as I said before, are notorious from one coast to the other. -Smuggling conditions there are worse than they are anywhere else on the continent, not excluding even Montreal, and yet nothing was said about them by the hon. member.
The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) in a very learned speech, also strove to impress upon us the viciousness of the administration of the Department of Customs. When the hon. gentleman was speaking, however, my mind went back to a period early in February when he told us about the hundreds of people in his community, in his own fair city, going out on the hillside in the depths of a Canadian winter and gathering grass to carry home as the only fuel they could get to keep them from freezing. That was a terrible state of affairs in a city where such an enormous quantity of beef, as stated by the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), is consumed. The hon. member for West Hamilton made a speech such as we might expect from a high class criminal lawyer. But some of it, I am afraid, resembled the product of a member of another profession in which I understand he is engaged, namely, that of playwright. In view of these two roles in which the (hon. member has distinguished himself, and bearing in mind also the picture he painted of the dismal conditions in Hamilton, we may be pardoned if we do not take his arguments too seriously on the present occasion.
The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has a highly trained legal mind. He applied his well known critical faculty, his great dialectical power, to attacking the government. I have often thought, while admiring the skill displayed by , the right hon. gentleman in building up his case, that that case is often laid on poor foundation. He reminds me of a critic who wishes to examine a picture, and who, instead of standing back from the painting and trying to view it in its proper perspective and proportions as the artist intended, goes right up to the picture, pulls out a thread from the canvas with a pair of pincers, examines that thread under a high-powered microscope and tears it completely to pieces. I have no complaint to make of that; it is the usual style of the right hon. gentleman, but it is regrettable that instead of taking a broad view of national conditions he limits himself to a very narrow and very sectional view. Therefore I am sure that his fine legal argument, spun out in great detail as it was, will not HOll-3211
affect public sentiment to the extent desired by my right hon. friend.
As regards smuggling and other crimes of a similar nature in this country I desire nothing more than to see the law thoroughly enforced; I desire nothing better than that there should be a thorough investigation into the administration of the Customs department, or any other department that may come under fire, at this or at any other time. It seems to me that it would be far better to have a judicial investigation, such as contemplated by the subamendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) into such matters than to throw the issue into a partisan assembly such as this. It is true we have power to try this and other matters except where they have not been handed over to the jurisdiction of the courts. In the last couple of weeks we had a striking reminder of this House, in an electoral case, having divested itself of its power and conferred it upon the properly constituted courts of the country. In the present instance, I think the same procedure should be followed. It is true that the House of Commons has a right to judge the government of the day on its merits. But when men are accused of law-breaking as distinct from unwise or inexpedient administration or leadership, surely the proper way to determine their innocence or guilt is by judicial procedure. Here we have charges made and the accusers are also the grand jury and the petty jury. Such a condition of affairs in any other transaction would be considered most unreasonable, and I know hon_ members will agree with me, even though they may be prevented from expressing their-views, that this is a most unreasonable course to take.
There is another consideration that I think should be kept in mind when discussing the relative merits of an investigation by a judicial body or by a partisan committee of the House. To-night we are putting ourselves in the position of sitting in judgment while only part of the evidence is in our -hands. The city of Montreal, Rock Island, Beebe and a few other isolated points have been investigated fairly thoroughly, but the rest of the Dominion from coast to coast has not yet been investigated. I am not criticizing the committee on this account, but I do say we should not sit in final judgment on this case, even if it be conceded that it is legal for us so to do, until all the evidence is before us. For that reason, if for no other, I think a judicial investigation should be proceeded with.
5066	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
The fundamental causes of smuggling have been already touched on. Undoubtedly when you make it profitable you will find a certain class of men ready to take the risks incident to smuggling. During the Napoleonic wars and for a few years afterwards smuggling was one of the greatest troubles of the British authorities, and men took desperate chances of fine and imprisonment .because of the big profits which attended successful smuggling operations. Not until the duties were reduced, and in many cases abolished, did the illicit traffic die out. Once the incentive to smuggling is removed, smuggling ceases. I have not heard during this investigation of anyone having been found guilty of smuggling farm machinery, coal oil, binder twine or similar commodities into this country of late years, simply because the duty is so low it is not worth the risk. Usually only high-priced commodities of small .bulk are handled by smugglers.
To-night, Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask hon. members to keep in mind that the things which loom so large before us at this time and seem so important to us in the heat and mist of partisan debate will in a few years shrink to their right proportions and appear of Little account. 1 am satisfied1 that then we will have forgotten who Moses Aziz was. His name will not be so much remembered as the name of the man mentioned by the Solicitor General when speaking yesterday. But one thing we will remember, whether the result of this debate was good or evil for the country as a whole. By that time, however it will be too late to change our decision.
During the debate I heard it charged that the Customs department deteriorated very rapidly in the last few years. I hold in my hand volume 52, part I of the public accounts for 1916, and I find that even at that time there was rapid deterioration going on in the Customs service. For instance, instructions were given at some ports, particularly at Morrisiburg, to allow certain articles to be entered free of duty, and those articles were brought in in car lots. I am not going to read the evidence, but it is at least interesting as showing that the deterioration of the Customs service has been going on for a long time.
The people of Canada to-night are more interested, Mr. Speaker, in seeing that the Customs department and every other department of government is improved and strengthened, and that the administration is conducted in such a way that it will enure to the prosperity and peace of the country, rather than in the case of Moses Aziz or any 
other smuggler on whose behalf members of parliament have been asking for clemency. Such requests are being made day after day of the authorities in Ottawa, Toronto and every other capital city in the Dominion, and many of them are granted. The people of Canada are not so much interested in clemency being granted or withheld, neither are they so much interested in the legal arguments advanced to-night; but they are interested in the result of this vote. To-night we are making our choice for the people of Canada, who are not able to come here to make it themselves, as to whether the government that has carried on during the past five years, the government that they know has helped greatly to bring back prosperity to Canada and to restore that condition of political and economic satisfaction that we have had in the past few years, shall be sustained.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton):
subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should not intervene at this late hour of the debate, but for the fact that on this question I think members generally on both sides of the House should voice their feelings. It is not a question, in essence, of any party issue. It is a question that transcends all party considerations and has to do, as the right hon. leader of the opposition said in his speech yesterday, with the honour of the country. May I say that in listening to the different speeches that were delivered in defence of the action of the Minister of Customs and in defence of the action, or rather the inaction, of the government, I think no one who afterwards reads the pages of Hansard will fail to come to the conclusion that the defence advanced by the ministers, even those most prominent and most interested, utterly failed to accomplish what it was proposed to accomplish. The pleas which were made were ad misericor-diam appeals, based on the inexperience of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin) so far as the charges relate to him, and upon the fact that he had only recently come into his office and was not familiar with the duties and powers belonging to it. Such a plea was put forward on behalf of a gentleman who, as has already been pointed out. had a distinguished legal career and a long practice not merely in civil law, because had that been the case we might have found some reason to explain and extenuate his conduct. But this is the conduct, the course of action of a lawyer not only brilliant and learned in his legal acquirements and in the practice of his profession but a lawyer whose practice has been in criminal law, who has been a prosecutor for the crown. The speech of the hon.

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bury
minister himself was a poor attempt to justify and explain his conduct; the speech of the Prime Minister, (Mr. Mackenzie King) his leader, was almost equally poor and weak and irrelevant; the speech of the Solicitor General might be placed in the same category for absolute inefficiency, and finally the speech of the Minister of Railways, who was supposed to take this House by storm and be the saviour of his party and of the country, was perhaps the poorest speech delivered by a member of the government that I have heard in the months I have been in this House.
Not merely was there an utter absence of genuine defence or argument but in point of fact there was gross misrepresentation by nearly all the gentlemen whose names I have mentioned, both of the facts and of the law. That statement is easy to make but perhaps not so easy in tihe time at my disposal to exemplify, but the misrepresentations in connection with the law were perfectly obvious. The Minister of Customs informed the House yesterday evening that it lay virtually with 'the Minister of Customs to issue his warrant of commitment before a man, found guilty by a magistrate or by two justices of tihe 'peace, should be taken to prison and confined there. That, of course, is utter rubbish. The warrant is not that of the Minister of Customs 'but one issued by the magistrate or justices who try the man. The Criminal Code of this country which, as the Solicitor General very well knew and as the Minister of Railways should have known, regulates procedure in these matters, directs the justices or the magistrate who tried the case, immediately after the conviction of the offender, to fill in the form of conviction according to the code and to issue a warrant according to the nature of the sentence.
Now let me pass on to some of the charges made in this case. I say-and I think the House will agree with me-that the charges have been absolutely proved. The charges which were laid by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) on February 2, have been proved practically to the hilt, as will be seen by the reports and findings of the special committee. Not only that, but we have the admission of one of the members of that committee, the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Don-aghy), in his long speech delivered the other day, that if the hon. member for Vancouver Centre had not taken the action he did these facts would never have been elicited, and the condition of the Department of Customs would never have been brought to light. It
follows, therefore, that all the attempts-and they have been many and strenuous and eloquent and vociferous-which have been made to throw discredit on the action of the hon. member, and the attempts to discredit the motives and results of his action are absolutely answered not out of the mouths of members on this side of the House but out of the mouth of the member appointed by the government on that committee.
I wish to say also that in his defence of the government the Prime Minister was very eloquent and very diffuse in laying before the House what the government had done, by reason of which they should be exonerated from these charges and sent back to resume their duties with a clean sheet. If you analyze the speech of the Prime Minister, the speech of the Solicitor General, even the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver North, and the speeches of most of the members who spoke on behalf of the government, you will find that the only defence is that the government placed adequate legislation on the statute books. The Prime Minister took us over one statute after another which was placed on the statute books by this government, directed to meet the needs of the Department of Customs. I submit to this House that the trouble is not with the legislation; the trouble is with the administration, and there was a very significant and very eloquent silence on the part of all government supporters who were so strenuous in their defence of the administration on the one vital matter of how the government administered their own statutes. It would be far better for this country if it had about one-half of the present statutes, and they were administered properly. There is no use trying to cure an evil of this kind by putting statutes on the statute book, to be filed away on the shelves of parliament or of our law societies or in legal offices or even on the shelves of ministers of the government. What this country wants is that the legislation that now exists on the statute books of this country shall be carried out fearlessly, without partiality, with a stern and determined hand, that the ill-doer shall be caught and punished to the last letter of the law, and when that is done the stigma that rests upon the fair name of this country -and that it does so rest, is shown by the facts that have been divulged as a result of this inquiry-will be lifted from that name.
Another thing to which I would like to call the attention of the House is this. The pleas that have been made here have been most absurd. The hon. member who preceded me, the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean)

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Bury
urged upon the House that there had been continuous efforts by the opposition to swing votes. That was the weight of one of the first charges he made against us, that we had been busy trying to swing votes. Oh, I should like to have the secret history of the last four months of this parliament! I should like to have told here all that went on behind closed doors in ministers' offices and in private members' offices throughout this building. I should like to know who did the trying to swing votes. I venture to say here and now that from the beginning of this session till this very day the government have been trying to swing votes to keep in office, and its tenure of office has been the most precarious tenure of office that any government has ever had. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we have
any more amendments, or subamendments, or any more votes recorded I desire to make

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Motherwell
a few observations. True it is that the subamendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodisworth) has been defeated, but the battle is never won or lost until the last gun is fired1. My mind goes back with some vividness to the night of February 2 last when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) made his famous charges against the government. Ever since then, however, hon. gentlemen opposite have kept rigidly away from the allegation with respect to the former Minister of Customs and Excise having taken away to his home at Three Rivers nine targe boxes of public documents and there destroyed them. At no time throughout the entire investigation has any attempt been made to ascertain whether such an allegation had any semblance of the truth. And yet throughout his speech the hon. member for Vancouver Centre repeated the allegation and asserted that if such a thing were true there was danger of more evidence of a damaging nature being destroyed. The House will recall that the question before us at the time was whether there should be an adjournment. The government was asking for an adjournment of six weeks in order to carry out the reconstruction of the cabinet. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre took the ground that in view of all these documents having been taken away from the files and destroyed, there was a possibility that other documents might be taken away and destroyed in the same ruthless manner if we were given an adjournment. That was the keynote of his statement; I remember it quite well. However, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre did not make his charges applicable to the government on, that occasion. He was good enough to absolve the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) from any complicity in this terrible crime, and he also absolved the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) and I remember quite well, too, that he was good enough to absolve myself from any complicity. I think I told my good friend on that occasion that I did not want any absolution at his hands.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I think the chief
charge contained in the amendment has been that this government has -been too slow in instituting reforms in connection with smuggling throughout Canada. Well, Mr. Speaker, if we have been Slow in this matter, all other governments have been slower still, because no other government since confederation ever took such prompt action to put down.' smuggling, and no government ever achieved the success that has attended our efforts.

Let us see what there is in this charge against the Minister of Customs. A few days after the general election last October we went into council and decided to carry on until parliament met and then ask whether we would be sustained in this House, with the result that on some fourteen or fifteen occasions we have been sustained by our supporters and our allies. Two or three days following the election of October 29, 1925 after we decided to carry on, the Minister of Customs consulted the Minister of Finance with regard to the best steps to take to combat this smuggling difficulty. At that time our desks were covered with accumulations of correspondence and papers which we had not been able to attend to during the campaign, but by November 15, the Minister of Customs had got in touch with Mr. Duncan, an ex-Scotland Yard detective whom the Minister of Finance had loaned him for the purpose of investigating conditions in Montreal and elsewhere. At the time Mr. Duncan had other investigatory work on hand, but by December 1 he was in Montreal prosecuting the inquiry that we felt was necessary before we took further action to combat the smuggling evil. No reasonable man can claim that the Minister of Customs could have acted more expeditiously.
In the meantime the member for Vancouver Centre seemed to know exactly what was taking place in the department. On the very day that Mr. Duncan got into harness at Montreal the member for Vancouver Centre, or some of his friends, sent a despatch to the Montreal Star intimating that he intended to take action in the matter-but he was just two weeks behind the Minister of Customs. It is significant that on February 2 the hon. member made allegations and charges against this government respecting the very conditions that are outlined in the report made by Mr. Duncan on the instructions of the Minister of Customs.
We all know the legal axiom that whoever seeks justice must come before the court with clean hands. Let us inquire how the hon. member for Vancouver Centre stands in that respect. First he puts himself in the dual position of investigator and prosecutor. Then when the committee was being formed he allowed himself to be put in the position of judge and juror. AVas there any impropriety there? AATat is the usual custom when one member makes a charge against another? If he is offered the opportunity of going on the committee, very often he declines for good and substantial reasons obvious to all. But the hon. member has no delicacies of that nature; he wants to be prosecutor; he wants to be judge and jury and now. if we

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Motherwell
allow him, he would like to be hangman as well. There are no niceties to deter the hon. member from cleaning up this mess and incidentally destroying the government.
There is another triviality; the hon. member gave no notice the night he made his statement. You will remember that the substance of his remarks was on the order paper in the form of a resolution; he took it off in the middle of the night and then, when other assassins were abroad, he launched it in the form of a charge against this government, taking the Minister of Customs entirely unawares and giving him no opportunity for preparation. But I suppose that is only a trivial oversight on the part of my hon. friend; if he were out to kill, why give notice? However, we will pass that up.
Then another thing is the method which he followed in getting his information. Where did it come from? Mr. Duncan in his evidence says it is his opinion that the information came from Mr. Sparks. I did not look it up, but an hon. gentleman informs me that Mr. Sparks swore that the information did not come from him. When the Minister of Customs intimated that he knew where my hon. friend got the information in the Duncan report, my hon. friend denied that. Then the Minister of Customs said:
Wild my 'hon. friends make the same denial concerning Mr. Sparks?
Then note the hon. member's answer:
No. Mr. Speaker, so far as the Merchants' Protective Assoteiartio-n is concerned it is, as the hon. minister knows, an association of business men which has met the government on several occasions. I have mert the Merchants' Proiteetive Association, as I have met Mr. Sparks, both last year and this year. But I want to say to the hon. minister that the information which I used to-day is certainly not exclusively or indeed in large measure that of Mr. Sparks.
He admits inferentially, however, that some of that information came from Mr. Sparks, although he does not say how much. I have not the pleasure of Mr. Sparks' acquaintance; I may meet him some time but just now I must form my opinion from what he has done not only in this regard but in other respects. Mr. Sparks swore that he did not give the information to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, while the hon. member admits in his speech that he received some of the information from Mr. Sparks. These two gentlemen cannot both be telling the truth, and I leave it to them to settle who is wrong. One thing which we do know, however, is that the hon. member had the substance of the Duncan report before the Minister of Customs ever saw it. That was information dug up at the instance of the minister, and the hon. member used it as a foundation for his charges. He
used it 'to destroy the future political prospects of the minister, and to destroy the government as well. Well, I suppose the question of ethics does not enter very much into warfare, but I think we might examine into what this means. If I know anything at all the information upon which the hon. member based his charges was stolen by somebody from somebody, and the hon. member used stolen goods; that is the way he started to clean up things, but we will see how it finishes.
What was the government going to do with this information when they got it? Judging from the attitude we have taken in the matter of royal commissions, as outlined in the amendment just defeated, we were going to take the course usually followed in matters of this kind. First we were going to have a parliamentary committee to look into these charges, something in the nature of a preliminary hearing before a magistrate. Then, if the allegations were reasonably substantiated, the matter would be submitted to a royal commission which would go into it in a judicial way and get at the real facts. But apparently the hon. member was desirous of precipitating a political issue; hon. members opposite did not want an investigation by a royal commission, because they have voted down a subamendment to that effect.
I remember some experiences I had which the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) mentioned this afternoon. He took the ground that if this government would only follow the example set by the Scott government of Saskatchewan in 1916, when they cleaned up the rascality found to exist in some departments there, as a supporter of that government he would be delighted to support this government as well. That is exactly the course that we started out to pursue. What was the result of the investigations at Regina? First of all, we had three committees appointed, and these three committees established the fact that great wrongs had been committed, that thefts had been committed by part of the staff. While we were hunting around for the personnel of three royal commissions to continue these investigations, there was a great deal of excitement among the ranks of the opposition, just as there is here to-day. They thought that we were going to leave the matter in the hands of a committee of the House and, as they said, whitewash ourselves. It took us some time to find enough judges available to constitute these three commissions, and what kind of judges did we appoint? Did we appoint judges who would Whitewash us? No. Did we appoint judges that we hoped would be

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: I want to point out that we not only started this investigation as soon as the Minister of Customs had taken office, but away back in 1924 we went out of our way to such an extent that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George said that we have abdicated all the functions of government in working in co-operation with the Commercial Protective Association, which had asked us to endeavour to clean up this smuggling business. We asked them what they wanted, and they said they wanted remedial legislation. We were busy in the midst of a session at the time, if I remember rightly, and we logically and properly answered: You draft the legislation, and if it is reasonable we will put it through. We also increased by a considerable amount the vote for the preventive service, so that the staff might be enlarged. When has there been in the history of Canada since confederation such an attempt to better matters, and yet we are going to be censured for what we did by the men who never did anything but help corrupt the situation and make it worse. If we are going to have a fight, we might as well have it on that as anything else. The one who does most to clean things up is going to be censured. But there is a higher court than this, Mr. Speaker, to appeal to, and that is the country, and we are not afraid to go there.

when we go to the country; they will not be able to get away with traducing remarks about Hon. Jacques Bureau taking his files away. Let us examine that file charge.

speechtext: What's the use of bothering? It won't do any good.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Let us examine it, because the ashes of those burned files-they said they were burnt-are rising up in judgment against hon. gentlemen opposite and proving them to be wrong. What about the letter from the liquor commission? That proves it was submitted to the liquor commission. It was said to be burned and destroyed, but I say it is rising up in judgment against hon. gentlemen opposite now. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition said: Well, if that letter was there, it should not have been there. It was a public document. But he did not tell the House that it was addressed to Three Rivers and never was forwarded to Ottawa. That might very easily happen. For many years when I was in Regina my home was in Abernethy, and sometimes I would have twenty or thirty letters there awaiting my arrival. It was very easy for these letters not to be forwarded to Regina. They might very easily be filed away by someone who did not know their purport, and so with Mr. Bureau. I wonder if the hon. member for Vancouver Centre really believed what he said. He should know that Mr. Bureau, like any other minister, had the right to take away his private files. Was he not a minister himself for three or four weeks in 1921? He must have known that he had the right, and I know he exercised the right of taking away some of these files because there was a file of the Department of Trade and Commerce put on the table during the debate on the contract of Sir William Petersen. The file was supposed to be on the table there. It was noticed by the right hon. leader of the opposition. There was a letter in that file marked "confidential". The Prime Minister indicated that it should not be tabled, and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) knew he had a right to that letter and took it off the file before our eyes; so that he knew Mr. Bureau had the right to take away his private files. The keystone of his charges was that boxes of letters were taken to Three Rivers and destroyed. He repeated the charge and opposed an adjournment for fear we would cover up our alleged nefarious conduct by the destruction of more files. Do hon. gentlemen think he can get away with that before a royal commission,
or before the electors-making charges that the minister has stolen property and also trying to ruin the reputation of an honourable man, the present Minister of Customs, whose shoestrings he is not fit to unloose? I do not quote poetry often, but here is a passage from Othello which I will read.
Wlho steals my punse steals trash.
And if we remain in Ottawa much longer, he who steals my purse will certainly steal trash. It reads:
The good name, in man and woman, dear my lord,
Is the immediate jewel of their souls.
Who steals my .punse, steals trash; '.tis something, nothing;
'T was mine, 't is his, and has been slave to thousands;
But he that filches from me my good name,
Robs me of that which not enriches him,
And makes me poor indeed.
The only difference is that he attempts to filch the good name of the hon. Minister of Customs, but that does enrich him, which makes the offence a thousand times worse. However, it does not seem to affect him, he is as hard as a nail, with a hide on him like a rhinoceros. I remember the night he made those charges. He did it well. He thought he was going to shake the members on this side of the House out of their chairs that night, and he came pretty nearly doing it, but those of us who know the hon. gentleman, the fearless fighter he has been in former sessions, can see the violent contrast between his conduct in former sessions and during this session. Ever since that night he has taken very little part in proceedings, but no doubt he did his work in the committee. As soon as he got through that night, as soon as he saw the hon. Minister of Customs was ready for him-which was not due to preparedness, because he did not know what was coming; it was rather due to his resourcefulness-he was able to meet him. I was reminded of the retreat from Mons; as soon as the enemy had dug in it was only a matter of time till he would be beaten. I want to draw a parallel in the present case. My hon. friend's march upon the Marne was stopped that night.
I forgot to tell the House the result of the investigation of the Regina commission. Some men were put in gaol and one sent to the penitentiary. Was the government ruined? We went to the country the next year, and in a House of sixty members seven Tories came back. Give us a chance to show the heinousness of the hon. member's charges. Let us have a royal commission, such as we had in Regina. Well, there may be more than

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Motherwell
seven Tories come back to this House, but they will have a very much smaller number than they have at the present time. If the hon. Minister of Customs and other young men on this side of the House, who are growing into prominence both inside and outside the government, have an opportunity to display their talents for one year, we will see what will happen. This government would be in power for an indefinite length of time and they may be in any event. What does the investigation show? It shows that it is very incomplete. It says that more inquiries' will be necessary. Yet think of it, wanting to render a decision, with the evidence only partly in! What would you think. Mr. Speaker, of a judge, hearing evidence on one side only, solemnly rendering a decision. The committee investigating this matter admit that the investigation was only partial and that subsequent investigation will be necessary to get at the real situation. Yet they want to render a verdict based on a partial exposure of the facts. It is just as reasonable as a judge on the bench giving a decision without hearing all the facts. Why does the opposition want that? Because they know that a complete exposure of the facts would put them in the wrong and put us in the right, so that there would be no hope for them at the next election. That is the reason they want a snap verdict.
I wish I could impress my Progressive friends with these facts. There are not many of them in the House at the moment. I know they are really desirous of doing the right thing. I ask them if it is right for members to base actions on party feelings. We are "ready, aye ready", for further investigation. Why is it not granted? Did we not make the best possible use of every particle of our time since the Minister of Customs came into the government and before that? How are we going to clean up all the mess which was left after the Tory government had been in power for ten years? This customs matter, is part of it. The charges against my colleague completely 'broke down. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) demonstrated that this afternoon. What is the charge? It is that this government is subject to censure, although any one member of this government has done more to improve matters than all the whole caboodle opposite. But I do not mind what the Tories do, I expect it. It is part of the game. What would they do if they followed their feelings? If one-tenth of those members who wanted to break away from the party on the motion for censure against the Minister 
of Customs acted as they really felt, we would not have been two behind but about twenty ahead. I know' how many men would have censured the Minister of Customs if he had been outside of politics and if they really desired to express their honest opinion. How many of them will get up alongside of him and size up to him in character and ability? I do not think there would be very many applicants. Lots of hon. members on the other side have character and ability, but there among them is no man of greater ability and promise than the Minister of Customs. They just want to get over here. It is a long time since the 29th October last to wait to get over here. They were just within the promised land as they thought, but they were denied entrance. They think they are just about in now. but they are not here yet.
This question involves many things. If the government and their allies are defeated, it means that we shall get a dissolution or somebody on the other side will be called upon. There is no doubt who will be called upon; it will be the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). The Montreal Star and the Gazette sometimes have had another guess, but they have always been guessing wrong, anid I do not think their guess has done the leader of the opposition any harm. When these party papers begin sniping their own leaders, they are not up to much. That applies to both sides; we have the same thing to contend with, so that that makes me sympathise with my right hon. friend.

The leader of the opposition when he was in the west pledged himself to the building of the Hudson Bay railway providing it would not cost more than $3,000,000. That pledge would be carried out if he gets into power to-morrow and the Hudson Bay railway would stop somewhere in the vicinity of where he stopped it before, namely at Kettle rapids, the second crossing of the Nelson river. I wonder bow supporters of the Hudson Bay railway axe going to justify before their electors defeating this government for having done more to suppress the smuggling evil and by their action jeopardizing the Hudson Bay railway. The leader of the opposition is going to have some trouble in defending that in Portage la Prairie if I know anything. I look forward with some interest to the contest in Portage la Prairie; I hope it will not be a three-cornered one. How much further will his supporters allow him to go than to spend the $3,000,000? Not one foot farther.
What about the grain bill that is hanging up in the Senate waiting for somebody to come that they do not want to come? Nobody on either side wants Mr. Boyd to come to Ottawa; they do not need him; but they are waiting for him to come. What will happen to that bill, commonly called the Campbell bill? When that bill was in the agricultural committee, every Liberal, every Progressive, every anti-Tory in the committee voted for it. It really should be called the Turgeon bill that should have been put through last year instead of now. Twelve Conservatives voted against it in the agricultural committee. It is now in the Senate; how much mercy is it going to receive from the party that is always behind the big interests-the Tory party? We shall see what the farmers have to say about that when they ask:	Why did you jeopardize these things?
What are you getting in lieu of this? Were the government and their allies not doing well enough for all parts of Canada, but particularly for the west and the Maritimes?
One of the things we have done for the Maritimes is to clean up tuberculosis in the
cattle. There is only one province in the Dominion that is free from tuberculosis as regards its cattle and that is Prince Edward Island. There is a standing offer to the Premier of Nova Scotia to do the same thing for that province just as soon as they are ready. That has not been done in any other province. We have in the estimates a provision, an old part of the Agricultural Act vote devoted to paying the balance of the instalments on two buildings in the Maritime provinces, one at Truro and one at Fredericton. That is something that has not been done for any other province.
What about the tariff, which means a great deal to us, if my right hon. friend comes over here? The tariff is of practically no use to western Canada. We recognize that we have to have a tariff; we are willing to have a reasonable tariff on what we have to buy; but we feel that the Maritimes and the prairie west that are really injured by a protective tariff should be dealt with fairly in order to compensate them for their loss under that tariff. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has to have revenue to carry on the government and this is one way in which something like $130,000,000 or $140,000,000 is secured. But it must be an equalized tariff, one that will bear as equally as possible on all classes of the people; and those who are not helped by it should have some compensation in lieu thereof. That has been our tariff policy. What has been the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite? Protection for the central provinces that have benefited most and let the rest of the country go hang. If the members from the Maritimes and the prairie provinces deliberately put their neck into this noose again they will do it with their eyes wide open. I wonder if my good friend the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) intends to run again. If he does not it is not because he is afraid to run; he is not afraid of anything. How is he going to explain his attitude toward these questions? That is what is interesting me?
We are going to have a very interesting election whether we are on the inside or the outside track. It is not always the horse on the inside track that wins the race; its the best horse that wins as a rule. The government has dealt with the tariff .in a manner most satisfactory to the country as a whole. There never has been such a satisfactory adjustment of the tariff since 1897 as there was this session. There has been an adjustment downwards of the income tax, restoration of the penny postage to the figure it was in 1897, a thing that was hailed with delight all over Canada. Are we to be punished for

Now it does not make one particle of difference to the revenue of this country whether the Quebec Liquor Commission buy that from the Customs department or from some distillery. I do not think the government are altogether blameless for the situation that is here tonight. I think they might have acted a little differently in the matter on the night of the 2nd of February when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was hurling his charges across the floor. I think the government should have got up then and told him in good plain English what they thought of him, even if they had to transgress the rules of the House. I would have done it. This committee, I say, did not investigate the charges. The charges are there, and they were not investigated. Why was the investigation confined to certain places and certain times? Well, everybody knows that the committee was composed of four Liberals, four Conservatives, and one Progressive. Everybody knows that the Liberals were suspicious of the Conservatives, that the Conservatives were suspicious of the Liberals, and that the Progressives did not trust either of them very much. The general attitude of the committee was that each side was trying to put something over the other. I reasoned when I saw the investigation had been confined to particular places and times desired by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre himself that it would be a very simple matter for the Conservative members of the committee to persist in asking questions and keeping the inquiry centred on any places they liked. The Liberal members of the committee could not object to that, because to do so would put them in the position of appearing to block the inquiry, so they had to allow those who were taking the initiative to centre the investigation pretty much where they liked.
The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell), who was a member of the committee, let a little more light on it this afternoon when he said that perhaps the Liberal members of he committee were asleep, implying that the Conservative members of the comfMr. Stevens.]
mittee were a little sharper than the Liberals and put something over them. That is the statement of a member of the committee, that the Conservatives acted in such a way as to put something over on the Liberals, and that is the evidence and that is the report on which we are asked to condemn the Minister of Customs, on the evidence of a committee a member of which says: Possibly the other side were asleep and we slipped something over on them. Is that justice?
Next we are told that the case is to be tried before this jury. This House is the court, and the members are the jury. The members of this House have not even read the evidence, which comprises some 3,000 pages, and a good many members have not even read the report. How then are we to judge this case. Can we be impartial judges? The jury itself is not in the court room. They have not read the evidence, they have not studied the report, and they have not been here during this debate. speechtext: It is a common practice for members of the House to request a minister to exercise clemency, and it is a common practice for the minister to exercise it. I will not ask the hon. gentleman if he has ever asked for it, but I say the time may come when he will do it, and be very glad to do it. We have a system of laws, and we have policemen to enforce the Jaws, but the policeman does not try an offender. He fakes him where he can be tried. We have a court to try offenders, and the offender can hire a lawyer to defend him, and if the case goes against him, and he has enough money, he can hire another lawyer to get him off. Is there any place where that man can find mercy? If there is not, it will 'be a sorry day for us. There must always be some place where the human element can come in, and where cold justice will not be the only con-sideratiioni. A long time ago it used to be the practice, when a general came back from the battlefield victorious, to honour him, but if he losft his army he was destroyed. That is considered barbarous to-day, and we do not do it any more. But here is another fight that is conducted along a line 4.000 miles in extent, and the general has 5,000 men under him, and because his forces were worsted at one or two outposts, you ask that the general himself be destroyed. It is the custom, I am told, among ship owners to discharge a captain who has lost his ship, but did you ever hear of them discharging a captain because for a single hour he had to run before the breeze? Never. Hon. gentlemen are great admirers of the tall chimneys and want them in all our cities. Do they not know that the tall chimneys sway in the wind. What would a tall chimney be if it were absolutely rigid and would not sway in the wind? It would snap and be worthless.

There is in the Customs department to-day the most capable, energetic and upright minister that has been there for many a long day, and because you find one grammatical error in his conduct you would condemn him. You know there are different kinds of men in the world. There is a big man, big-hearted, big-minded, who grasps big things in a big way, who can safely handle big affairs, and then there is the small strict man who never would go one hair's breadth out of the path of rectitude, and to-day we may choose. Will you have George Boivin, the big man, or the strict man who acts according to his formula? France had a strict man once who would not deviate one iota from the right path. It was the bloodthirsty Robespierre, the man that had no heart, no soul, nothing but the letter of the law and cold steel. That would not be the man to put in charge of any big affair or large department. How will the people of the country look at our action in this matter? We are told that the eyes of all Canada are centered on us. I think the hon. member said the other night that in all future generations they would be looking on us, when the walls of this building were crumbling into ruins and our names would stand out and it would be known how we voted. O wad some power the giftie gie us,

I was entirely alone. I heard his speech and his language was excellent. I understand him perfectly well. I congratulate him on his effort to acquire the French language, and should he wish to persevere in studying that language I know he will be able to come into our province to give us better reasons than those he gave us for having abstained from visiting us before the general elections.
I frankly admit, Sir, that when the hon. member for Vancouver Centre delivered his speech and spoke to us about people having been hung, murderers and robbers, the little hair I have on my head stood on end. We shivered, Sir, on hearing these charges. I thought: What, destroy public documents! There is not a member of the House who could be elected if he approved of such scandal. To charge the minister of having destroyed files, I say that it is the most formidable charge which can be levied against a public man who holds cabinet rank! Where would be our trust in public men, Sir, if ministers to hide their evil deeds, were to destroy the public files? For I acknowledge to the opposition the right to criticize. It is not without reason that the country pays to the leader of the opposition a salary of $14,000, it is that he may criticize justly. And, to his honour, I must acknowledge that he well earns his money, and if it depended on me I would wish him heartily to remain for a long time the leader of the opposition, in order that he might continue to criticize as he does with such ability the deeds of the government.
However, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has gone beyond the limit, he failed to substantiate his charge and it seems to me he owes the minister, not only on his account, but for the sake of his family, he owes him at least an apology or a public statement. If these charges had been made on the steps of the Chateau Laurier or anywhere else outside of this House, an action for damages would have been instituted by the minister so charged. I state that this is not courageous, that it is not generous to make such a charge when no proof is forthcoming; at least when we are aware that a false accusation has been laid, an

Is this the crowing of the rooster? The debate on the amendment-I am in order, Sir, I am speaking on the amendment the whole time-the debate on the amendment will perhaps last until to-morrow. Perhaps it may end before. We have munitions to carry on. I see here gallant warriors, sharpshooters, if you will have it so, and who will, when I am through, empty their belts. However, I would request at this early hour when dawn approaches and invites one to prayers, I would ask the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to place his hand on his conscience and think:	Do I not
owe an apology to the hon. minister whom I have vilified and against whom I have not substantiated my charges? I appeal to his heart and reason, and I feel convinced that before this session is over we shall have this apology. I think it is in the interest of the hon. member, humanity is the same all over, it has horror of injustice.
Now, Sir, I see that a number of members around me seem keen to take part in the debate. I have but one word to add. If the discussions in our public meetings were less bitter and especially in our parliaments, the public interest would be better served and the country would reap the benefit. I state that our public men have everything to lose in throwing mud at one another. I make such a statement on behalf of the good name of our country, because to-day, through the means of telegraph, these charges made in the nation's parliament do not remain there, they reach every part of the country, the United States, the old continent, and when we ask these people to send us their sons to help us in tilling the land of Canada, they answer: "But we are not going to emigrate to your country, the public funds can no further be trusted, public documents are no more in safety in your country, they are in the hands of political robbers." That is the effect produced in foreign lands by these non-substan-

tiated charges and 1 protest in the name of justice, honesty and in the interest of my country against these charges laid with a political aim and not substantiated nor retracted.
I shall close these few remarks, Sir, and I thank you for your kind attention. On the day of the celebration of the French Canadian national holiday, I conceived the idea of going together with a few friends to make a pilgrimage to the Notre-Dame cemetery. On entering we were faced with a magnificent mausoleum. Cut in the stone there was but one inscription, but one name Laurier. Surmounting it, there were nine women of bronze representing the nine provinces of the Dominion. The faces of all these women have different countenances but in each of these countenances, one can discover a common impression of sadness. They weep over tlhe one who has left us, the one who held the respect of all his fellow-citizens from the Atlantic to the Pacific. They weep over the man who gave more than fifty years of his life to his country; they weep over the one who gave fifteen years of prosperity and national grandeur to Canada which he loved so much. Union at death's door is an admirable thing. Indeed, union at death's door is a magnificent spectacle, but union in national life is still more beautiful. Canadians, hailing from Scotland, you that have preserved in your character something of the granite of its mountains; sons of the Emerald island; you that have left the shores of the proud Albion, and have preserved the motto of Trafalgar and are proud of it; you that have come from the sunny shores of old France, finally, you Canadians who have gathered from everywhere, let us put our shoulder to the wheel and let us work in the interest of the country; let us cease our fraticidal struggles, let us unite in brotherhood and justice.
